Mushrif and al-Zurq appear to be place names; their locations and vocalizations are uncertain. The elliptical ولا مي إلا أن تزور is understood as denying Mayy’s presence and leaving only a visit to her deserted campsites.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 1
Was it a campsite’s traces between al-Qilāt and Shāriʿthat made you yearn like a youth, until your eye kept shedding tears?
أمن دمنة بين القلات وشارعتصابيت حتى ظلت العين تدمع

Al-Qilāt and Shāriʿ are unidentified place names, repeated in line 7. The vocalization al-Qilāt is tentative.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 1
Is it because of an abandoned campsite in the hollow, Jaww Jalājil,that your companion streams with tears and is distraught?
أمن دمنة بالجو جو جلاجلزميلك منهل الدموع جزوع؟

Jaww Jalājil appears to name a hollow or tract of low ground associated with Jalājil; its precise location is uncertain.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 2
I defied love on the day at al-Qilāt, though on the day at al-Naqā I listened eagerly to love’s call.
عصيت الهوى يوم القلات وإنني لداعي الهوى يوم النقا لسميع

The place names القلات and النقا are rendered al-Qilāt and al-Naqā; their precise locations, and the vocalization of the first, are uncertain.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 4
Will those days of ours return, O Mayy—those at Dhū al-Rimth—or not? Is there no returning for them?
أراجعة يا مي أيامنا الألىبذي الرمث، أم لا مالهن رجوع؟

The precise location of Dhū al-Rimth is uncertain.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 1
May the two deserted campsites, whose like we have never found, be watered—yours at Ḥaql, O ʿAzz, which have adorned Ḥaql—
سقى دمنتين لم نجد لهما مثلابحقل لكم يا عز قد زانتا حقلا

Ḥaql is taken as a place-name; its precise location is uncertain.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 1
O Dārat al-Salam, to whose eastlie old encampment traces whose doves keep making us weep!
يا دارة السلم التي شرقيهادمن يظل حمامها يبكينا

Dārat al-Salam is an unidentified locality; the precise vocalization of السلم is uncertain.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 4
Dwellings of Mayy at Wahbayn, wateredby heavy showers, their clouds drizzling, and their [itmihmām].
منازل من مي بوهبين جادهاأهاضيب طل دجنها واتمهامها

Wahbayn (وهبين) is treated as a place name, but its identification and vocalization are uncertain.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 1
Stop by the campsite traces, long since abandoned,at al-Jizʿ, where time has stripped away their beauty.
ألمم على دمن تقادم عهدهابالجزع واستلب الزمان جمالها

Al-Jizʿ may be a place-name or a topographical description meaning the bend or winding course of a valley.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 1
Ruins of Zaynab’s camp, from before separation droveZaynab and Laʿūb away from Dhū al-Arāk.
دمن لزينب قبل تشريد النوىمن ذي الأراك بزينب ولعوب

I take Laʿūb as a second woman’s name. The precise location of Dhū al-Arāk is uncertain.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 3
May al-Ghaḍā and those who dwelt there be watered, though theykindled its fire within ribs and hearts.
فسقى الغضى والساكنيه وإن همشبوه بين جوانح وقلوب

Al-Ghaḍā may be a place-name or refer to a stand of ghaḍā trees. The following phrase, literally 'they kindled it,' evokes the burning of their wood.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 1
O Lord, take me, take ʿAlī, and take“O wind, what are you doing to the traces of the encampments?”
يا رب خذني، وخذ عليا، وخذيا ريح ما تصنعين بالدمن

The second hemistich appears to quote the opening of the poem being mocked, making that poem the third object of “take.” I could not identify the quoted poem or establish who ʿAlī is.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 1
Whenever the eyes recognize the traces of a campsite,Laylā’s, in upper Dhū Maʿarik, they weep—
متى تعرف العينان أطلال دمنةلليلى بأعلى ذي معارك تدمعا

Dhū Maʿarik appears to be a place-name; I cannot identify its location.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 5
I looked as the laden camels departed, and they drew abreastof Rakwa and the valley, while her riding camels moaned.
نظرت وقد زال الحمول، ووازنوابركوة والوادي وحنت ركابها

Rakwa (ركوة) is an unidentified place; its vocalization is uncertain. الوادي is translated literally as “the valley,” though it might designate a particular named locality.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 6
“Ah, for love of ʿAfrāʾ, how dear is the confluenceof Naʿām and Birk, where the two meet!”
ألا حبذا من حب عفراء ملتقىنعام، وبرك، حيث يلتقيان

Naʿām and Birk appear to be two valleys. The vocalization of برك, rendered here as Birk, is uncertain.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 1
Whose camp-trace is this at al-Naʿf, its ground effaced,its remnants altered, its freshness worn away?
لمن دمنة بالنعف عاف صعيدهاتغير باقيها ومح جديدها

Al-Naʿf may be a place name or a descriptive term for sloping ground beside a mountain or valley.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 2
Saʿda’s, from the year of al-Hurayma, when between usthere was affection, and her turning away had not yet distressed us.
لسعدة في عام الهريمة إذ بناتصاف، وإذ لما يرعنا صدودها

I could not identify the event or period called ‘the year of al-Hurayma’; the vocalization of الهريمة is uncertain.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 1
Whose campsite lies desolate at al-Janāb,extending to the slope, between al-Malā and the hills?
لمن دمنة أقفرت بالجنابإلى السفح بين الملا فالهضاب

Al-Janāb and al-Malā are treated as place names; their precise locations here are uncertain. Al-safḥ, translated as 'the slope,' may also be a place name.

On traces (rasm), line 1
The traces at Rāmah have faded, and in the ravines,and on the dunes of al-Ḥuḍayr as far as Lifāʿ.
عفا رسم برامة فالتلاعفكثبان الحضير إلى لفاع

The places الحضير and لفاع are not securely identified; the vocalizations al-Ḥuḍayr and Lifāʿ are tentative. التلاع is taken as the common noun 'ravines,' though it could be a place name.

On traces (rasm), line 1
Did the traces at al-Naqʿ stir your longing this morning—effaced, their last days of habitation long ago?
أشاقتك بالنقع الغداة رسومدوارس أدنى عهدهن قديم

Al-Naqʿ is taken as a place-name; its location is uncertain. أدنى عهدهن may refer to the most recent habitation of the sites or the speaker’s last acquaintance with them.

On traces (rasm), line 4
They became like a striped cloak torn apart:one packing up and leaving at dawn, another staying behind.
فعادوا كبرد العصب شق فأصبحوافمحتمل غاد، وظل مقيم

وظل مقيم is read as 'and another remained.' Without vocalization, ظل could instead be the noun 'shade,' yielding 'a lingering shade.'

On traces (rasm), line 1
The campsite’s familiar traces stirred my heart,desolate at Dhū al-Haḍabāt, like a tattoo.
هاج الفؤاد معارف الرسمقفرا بذي الهضبات كالوشم

Dhū al-Haḍabāt appears to be a place-name; its location is uncertain.

On traces (rasm), line 3
I kept concealing my feelings, until it was as thoughat Dhū al-Ramth they had never crossed anyone’s mind,
فما زلت أطوى النفس حتى كأنهابذي الرمث لم تخطر على بال خاطر

The feminine pronoun in كأنها has an uncertain referent. The translation takes it to refer to النفس, understood here as the speaker’s inward feelings; a reference to an unmentioned beloved is also possible. Dhū al-Ramth is treated as a place-name, but its location is unidentified.

On traces (rasm), line 2
May the sands of al-Ḥimā and the traces of the abode atal-Liwā be watered by a thundering cloud, delighting with what it pours.
سقى رمل الحمى ورسوم مغنى اللوى هزج يروق بما يريق

The locations intended by al-Ḥimā and al-Liwā are uncertain. Al-Ḥimā may instead mean simply 'the protected pasture.'

On traces (rasm), line 1
Long have I lingered by the traces at Tamthūd;they have perished—and all that is new must one day perish.
طال الثواء على رسم بتمثودأودي، وكل جديد مرة مود

Tamthūd (تمثود) is an unidentified place; its vocalization is uncertain.

On traces (rasm), line 3
at Jaww, as though you had never dwelt there, nor had there beendesert camps and settlements by the water for your people around it.
بجو كأن لم تحتلله، ولم يكنلأهلك مبدي حوله ومحاضر

Jaww (جو) may be a place-name here, but the word can also mean a low-lying tract or broad valley.

On traces (rasm), line 1
Say, you two, to the surviving trace of Maylāʾ’s dwelling at al-Liwā—Liwā al-Haḍb, between al-Maghr and al-Mutakharram:
فقولا لباقي رسم ميلاء باللوىلوى الهضب بين المغر والمتخرم

The places are unidentified; the vocalizations al-Haḍb, al-Maghr, and al-Mutakharram are provisional.

On traces (rasm), line 4
Then distance carried those dwellings far from you, and nowthe heights of Raḍwā and Tasūm lie between you and them.
فشطت نوى عنك الديار فأصبحتمناصب رضوى دونها وتسوم

مناصب is rendered tentatively as ‘heights’; its precise topographical sense here is uncertain. تسوم (Tasūm) appears to be a mountain name, but its identification is uncertain.

On traces (rasm), line 1
Do you shun a fresh trace of Suʿād’s dwelling?Her dwelling at Rawḍat al-Ajdād has faded away, and at Yathqub too.
أرسما جديدا من سعاد تجنبعفت روضة الأجداد منها فيثقب

I take تجنب as a second-person verb, ‘do you shun.’ Rawḍat al-Ajdād and Yathqub appear to be place names; their precise identification and vocalization are uncertain.

On traces (rasm), line 1
O timeworn trace of a dwelling, were there not oncecontented folk within you, and horses roaming,
ألا أيها الرسم المحيل ألم تكنبك الأنس الراضون والخيل رودا

رودا is taken to describe horses roaming or grazing; its precise vocalization and grammatical connection are uncertain.

On traces (rasm), line 2
And fair maidens gathered together, as though they werewild does of al-Malā, wearing fine wraps and saffron-dyed cloth?
وبيض العذارى في جميع، كأنهانعاج الملا يلبس ريطا ومجسدا

الملا is taken as the place-name al-Malā, though it can also denote an open plain. مجسدا is understood as saffron-dyed cloth; a differently vocalized form can mean a garment worn next to the skin.

On traces (rasm), line 1
Has a spring campsite at al-Tanāṣuf stirred your longing, or not,and a desolate trace on the sandy flats of al-Ghadīrayn?
أهاجك أم لا بالتناصف مربعورسم بأجراع الغديرين بلقع

Al-Tanāṣuf and al-Ghadīrayn are treated as place names; their precise locations are uncertain.

On traces (rasm), line 1
From ʿAzza’s days at Dhū al-Ghuṣn, I was stirredby traces in the open hollow of al-Rawḍatayn.
لعزة من أيام ذي الغصن هاجنيبضاحي قرار الروضتين رسوم

Dhū al-Ghuṣn and al-Rawḍatayn are treated as place names; their precise locations are uncertain. قرار may mean a hollow or low-lying, level ground.

On traces (rasm), line 1
Come, greet the deserted traces at al-Zurq,though they are nothing but crumbling, weathered remains.
ألا حي بالزرق الرسوم الخوالياوإن لم تكن إلا رميما بواليا

Al-Zurq appears to be a place-name; its precise identification is uncertain.

On remains (āthār), line 1
Was it firelight that appeared to your eyes, or was there kindledat Dhū al-Athl a fire of Salāma’s?
ضوء نار بدا لعينيك أم شببت بذي الأثل من سلامة نار

Dhū al-Athl is an unidentified place.

On remains (āthār), line 2
There, among the meadows, tamarisks, and bān trees,is a dwelling once ours and Salāma’s.
تلك بين الرياض والأثل والبانات منا ومن سلامة دار

الرياض والأثل والبانات are translated as landscape terms ('meadows, tamarisks, and bān trees'); some or all may instead be place-names: Al-Riyāḍ, al-Athl, and al-Bānāt.

On remains (āthār), line 2
Heighten my longing with wine, and sing to me:“How grievous to me is parting from companions!”
زدني اشتياقا بالمدام وغننيأعزز علي بفرقة القرناء

The second hemistich appears to quote words to be sung; I could not identify a source for the possible quotation.

On remains (āthār), line 1
May your mornings be fair after our departure, and may you flourish,O dwelling of Ṣafrāʾ at al-Anʿam.
عمي صباحا بعدنا وانعمييا دار صفراء على الأنعم

Ṣafrāʾ is taken as a woman's name and al-Anʿam as a place-name; their identities are uncertain.

On residences, stopping places, haunts, landmarks, waymarks and courtyards, line 1
Laylā has dwellings to the east of al-Nijād,desolate, effaced by the north wind and persistent rain.
لليلى بشرقي النجاد مساكنقفار تعفتها شمال وداجن

النجاد may be a place name, rendered here as al-Nijād, or simply the plural of najd, meaning uplands.

On residences, stopping places, haunts, landmarks, waymarks and courtyards, line 1
I visited Laylā’s dwellings at al-Burūd,grown old, with the ages sweeping over them.
غشيت لليلى بالبرود مساكناتقادمن واستنت عليها الأعاصر

The precise identification and vocalization of البرود, rendered al-Burūd, are uncertain.

On residences, stopping places, haunts, landmarks, waymarks and courtyards, line 1
Is it every day, from lingering love,that you gaze toward the lofty peaks of Maylāʾ?
أفي كل يوم أنت من غبر الهوىإلى الشم من أعلام ميلاء ناظر؟

Maylāʾ appears to be a place name, but I could not identify its location or confirm its vocalization.

On residences, stopping places, haunts, landmarks, waymarks and courtyards, line 1
What stirred your longing among the familiar traces of the campsiteof al-Barq, amid stony ground and barren uplands?
ما هاج شوقك من معارف عرصةالبرق بين أصالف وفدافد

I take البرق as a place name, provisionally vocalized al-Barq; its identification and vocalization are uncertain. أصالف and فدافد are taken as terrain terms, 'stony ground' and 'barren uplands,' rather than place names.

On the land (arḍ), line 2
What fault is mine if I love my people's landand hate the tamarisks of al-Quṣayba?
فما لي إن أحببت أرض عشيرتيوأبغضت طرفاء القصيبة من ذنب

The place القصيبة, provisionally vocalized al-Quṣayba, has not been securely identified.

On the land (arḍ), line 3
If a wind could convey the words of a senderfull of affection, I would confide in the south wind at al-Naqb.
ولو أن ريحا بلغت وحي مرسلحفي لناجيت الجنوب على النقب

النقب is treated here as the place name al-Naqb, but it could instead mean 'the mountain pass.'

On the land (arḍ), line 1
An exile at al-Marj weeps in his grief,for those who comforted him in love have departed.
ومغترب بالمرج يبكي لشجوهوقد بان عنه المسعدون على الحب

Al-Marj literally means “the meadow.” It appears to be a place name here, but the specific location is uncertain.

On the land (arḍ), line 1
I had ceased to yearn for Najd, but I was stirredto remember it by al-Khaffān and al-Ḥuḍan.
قد كنت أقصرت عن نجد فهيجنيعلى تذكرها الخفان والحضن

The vocalization and identification of الخفان, rendered al-Khaffān, are uncertain.

On the land (arḍ), line 2
Dwellings that lamented the parting of those who journeyed awaythrough their colors, and adorned themselves with yellow flowers.
ديارا شكت فرقة الظاعنين بألوانها فتحلت بهارا

بهار denotes a flowering plant, often identified as a yellow oxeye or a kind of narcissus; the precise botanical identification is uncertain.

On the land (arḍ), line 1
I exchanged Dūdān for Ḥamal and its land,but neither my drink nor my drinking place pleased me.
تعوضت من دودان حملا وأرضهافما طاب لي شربي ولا راق مشربي

The identities of دودان and حمل are uncertain; Dūdān and Ḥamal are provisional vocalizations. Dūdān may designate a tribe rather than a place.

On the land (arḍ), line 3
When we part, we are rid of harm,and the shepherd pasturing his flock has no need to mark them.
إذا ما تفرقنا خلصنا من الأذىولم يحتج الراعي المسيم إلى الوشم

الوشم ordinarily means tattooing. Here it apparently means marking livestock for identification, though الوسم would be the more usual word for branding animals. The precise connection between this pastoral image and 'when we part' is uncertain.

On homelands (awṭān), line 1
Greet Qaṭan, if you know it well,with the greeting of one who once loved Qaṭan.
سلم على قطن إن كنت تألفهسلام من كان يهوى مرة قطنا

Qaṭan is probably the mountain of that name in Najd, though the identification is uncertain.

On homelands (awṭān), line 1
The sands are never mentioned but an exile yearns,whose heart’s desires and homes lie in Dhū al-Raml.
لا يذكر الرمل إلا حن مغتربله بذي الرمل أوطار وأوطان

Dhū al-Raml is treated as a place name, but its location is unidentified; the expression could also describe a sandy tract.

On homelands (awṭān), line 2
My heart’s longings flutter toward the bān trees;it is not the bān trees that move me, but the one whose home is there.
يهفو إلى البان من قلبي نوازعهوما بي البان، بل من دارهالبان

The joined text «دارهالبان» is read as «داره البان», ‘whose home is the bān trees.’ bān denotes the moringa tree, though al-Bān could here be a place name.

On homelands (awṭān), line 1
Can the nights at al-Munaqqā return,as they were for me when we were all together?
هل لليالي بالمنقى رجوعمثلما كن لي ونحن جميع

The place المنقى is unidentified here; its vocalization as al-Munaqqā is tentative.

On homelands (awṭān), line 2
Ḥabīb is dear to my heart for saying:“Perhaps a homeland will bring them near—perhaps.”
حبيب إلى قلبي حبيب لقوله:عسى وطن يدنو بهم، ولعلما

Ḥabīb probably refers to Abū Tammām, Ḥabīb ibn Aws. I have not securely identified the quoted verse; its concluding ولعلما is an elliptical expression of hope, rendered “perhaps.”

On homelands (awṭān), line 1
My young she-camel yearned in ʿAdān for Najd;the long passage of time had not made her forget her homeland.
حنت قلوصي في عدان إلى نجدولم ينسها أوطانها قدم العهد

عدان is treated as a place name, provisionally transliterated ʿAdān; its vocalization and precise location are uncertain.

On homelands (awṭān), line 3
Shall I ever make my hand a cushion for my cheekat Shaʿbaʿb, between al-Ḥawḍ and al-ʿAṭan?
هل أجعلن يدي للخد مرفقةعلى شعبعب بين الحوض والعطن؟

The vocalization of Shaʿbaʿb is uncertain. Al-Ḥawḍ and al-ʿAṭan are treated as place names, but they could mean ‘the watering trough’ and ‘the camels’ resting place by the water.’

On homelands (awṭān), line 2
A man bears them across the wilderness’s breadth, clothedin robes of praise, his ragged garments torn.
يطوى بهم عرض الفلاة مسربلحلل الثناء ممزق الأطمار

يطوى is read as يطوي, ‘he traverses’ or ‘bears across,’ with مسربل, ‘one clothed,’ as its subject. The person described is not explicitly identified; the transmitted spelling also permits a passive reading, which leaves the syntax less clear.

On homelands (awṭān), line 2
Depart when your homeland turns hostile;for even fresh aloeswood is firewood in its native land.
وارحل إذا كانت الأوطان نابيةفالمندل الرطب في أوطانه حطب

Al-mandal denotes a fragrant Indian wood, variously identified as aloeswood or sandalwood; the precise identification is uncertain.

On homelands (awṭān), line 3
In a gathering whose sight delights those who behold it,I have two sweet companions from Ḥulwān.
في مجلس تبهج الرائين رؤيتهولي قرينان من حلوان حلوان

Ḥulwān is a place-name borne by several localities; which one is intended is uncertain.

On cities (mudun), line 1
I said to al-Zabbāʾ, when it had comewithin reach of Time’s fang and claw—
قد قلت للزباء لما أصبحتفي حد ناب للزمان ومخلب

Al-Zabbāʾ is described here as a city; its precise identification is uncertain.

On cities (mudun), line 5
“Al-Madīnah is no city for us; keep, then, tothe sand-ridge of al-Sinād and the peak of al-Ājām,
إن المدينة لا مدينة فالزميحقف السناد، وقنة الاجام

The places al-Sinād and al-Ājām are unidentified, and their vocalization is uncertain. “For us” is supplied in interpreting the elliptical إن المدينة لا مدينة, literally “al-Madīnah is no city.”

On countries (bilād), line 1
Ah, would that I knew: shall I drive my she-camelthrough Bayḍāʾ Najd, where she used to travel?
ألا ليت شعري هل أسير ناقتيببيضاء نجد حيث كان مسيرها

بيضاء نجد may be a place name, Bayḍāʾ Najd, or simply mean 'the white plain of Najd'; the locality is uncertain.

On countries (bilād), line 1
Ah, is there a way to urge the swift she-camels on at midmorningand breathe the scent of lavender at al-Ghuwayr?
ألا هل إلى نص النواعج بالضحىوشم الخزامى بالغوير سبيل؟

Al-Ghuwayr is a place name, but its precise location is uncertain.

On countries (bilād), line 3
The lands of my people—by the Almighty, I love them—though I have become certain we shall not meet.
بلاد جميع، والعظيم أحبهموإن كنت قد أيقنت ألا تلاقيا

بلاد جميع is ambiguous. I have taken جميع as a company of people, understood here as her own people, but it might instead be a proper name, Jamīʿ. والعظيم is read as an oath, “by the Almighty.”

On countries (bilād), line 1
We found that our father had settled in a landmidway between Qays—Qays ʿAylān—and al-Fizr.
وجدنا أبانا كان حل ببلدةسوى بين قيس قيس عيلان والفزر

سوى بين is understood as 'midway between,' though the construction is uncertain. Al-Fizr may designate Saʿd ibn Zayd Manāt of Tamīm and, by extension, his descendants; the identification is uncertain.

On countries (bilād), line 5
May rain water Ṣaḥrāʾ al-Ihāla, a spring encampment,and al-Waqbā—what a soft-soiled, fertile dwelling!
فسقيا لصحراء الإهالة مربعاوللوقبي من منزل دمث مثرى

I could not securely identify Ṣaḥrāʾ al-Ihāla or al-Waqbā. The latter is printed الوقبي; its rendering assumes الوقبى.

On countries (bilād), line 3
May the clan settle at Jarʿāʾ Wāṣil,and may separation bring back those who have departed.
عسى أن يحل الحي جرعاء واصلوعل النوى بالظاعنين تريع

Jarʿāʾ Wāṣil appears to be a place-name, literally 'the sandy tract of Wāṣil'; I could not identify the location.

On countries (bilād), line 2
Nor do I love lands where I have seenʿAns, or a land where Qudam have settled.
ولا أحب بلادا قد رأيت بهاعنسا، ولا بلدا حلت به قدم

قدم is taken as the tribal name Qudam; its precise vocalization is uncertain.

On countries (bilād), line 2
How lovely, when the evening wind turns cold,is Wādī Ushayy, and the generous young men there.
وحبذا حين تمسي الريح باردةوادي أشى وفتيان به هضم

The description هضم is uncertain; it may mean 'slender-bellied' rather than 'generous.' The place name أشى is read as Ushayy.

On countries (bilād), line 1
May Ayāfith, among all lands, be wateredby the downpour of evening and morning clouds.
سقيت أيافث من بلادصوب الروائح والغوادي

أيافث is apparently a place name, provisionally transliterated Ayāfith; its identity and vocalization are uncertain.

On countries (bilād), line 1
O Wādī al-ʿAlajān, rejoiceat a flash of lightning over Wādī al-Ghamīm.
ألا يا وادي العلجان أبشرببارقة على وادي الغميم

Wādī al-ʿAlajān is not securely identified; the vocalization of its name is uncertain.

On countries (bilād), line 1
While darkness lay with its neck laid low, there flasheda gleam between Ṣāḥa and al-ʿArān.
تألق والدحى ملقى الجرانبريق بين صاحة فالعران

Ṣāḥa and al-ʿArān are unidentified place names; their vocalization is uncertain.

On countries (bilād), line 3
Then she said to maidenslike the gazelles of al-Rahīn:
م قالت لفتيات كآرام الرهين:

الرهين is treated as a place name, provisionally vocalized al-Rahīn; its identification and reading are uncertain.

On countries (bilād), line 2
is a mighty host that shatters the skullsof men beneath its cloud of dust.
دهم تفض جماجم الأقوام تحت قتامه

دهم can mean a great host or, with different vocalization, dark horses. I have chosen 'a mighty host'; the masculine suffix in قتامه ('its dust') favors this reading.

On countries (bilād), line 1
May the land of Ayāfith be wateredby downpours from evening and morning clouds.
سقيت أيافث من بلادصوب الروائح والغوادي

أيافث appears to be a place name, provisionally transliterated Ayāfith; its identification and vocalization are uncertain.

On countries (bilād), line 1
It delights my eyes to see, in her country,the crests of the clustered dunes of long-stretching al-Abraq;
يقر بعيني أن أرى من بلادهاذرى عقدات الأبرق المتقاود

I take عقدات as clustered dunes or sandhills, though it can also denote densely wooded patches. Al-Abraq is unidentified here; the word can also describe terrain mingling rock and sand rather than a specific place.

On countries (bilād), line 1
It gladdens my eyes to see, among her lands,Damāj, and to have al-Ajādiʿ come into view.
يقر بعيني أن أرى من بلادهادماجا، وأن تبدو لعيني الأجادع

I could not securely identify Damāj (دماج) or al-Ajādiʿ (الأجادع); the vocalization of Damāj is uncertain.

On the house (dār), line 1
I recognized the dwelling, deserted yet unchanged,between Ajyād Khifāf and al-Raḥl.
وقد عرفت الدار قفرا لم تحلبين أجياد خفاف فالرحل

I take لم تحل to mean 'unchanged,' though the unvocalized wording also permits a reading connected with habitation. The places are unidentified; the vocalization and grouping of أجياد خفاف فالرحل are uncertain.

On the house (dār), line 1
Ah, greet Rahbā, then greet al-Maṭālī:once a place of company, it now lies empty.
ألا حي رهبي ثم حي المطاليفقد كان مأنوسا فأصبح خاليا

I read رهبي as the place name Rahbā (رهبى), and المطالي as al-Maṭālī. Their precise locations are uncertain.

On the house (dār), line 2
Or can a weeping man be blamed, his tears stirredat al-Ḥijr, when the longing he feels has wasted him?
أم هل يلامن باك هاج عبرتهبالحجر إذ شفه الوجد الذي يجد؟

The place الحجر is provisionally read as al-Ḥijr; its identification and vocalization are uncertain.

On the house (dār), line 6
Of what you entrusted to me on the day at Dhū ʿAdham,I am a keeper, though the years grow long for the one entrusted.
إني لما استودعتني يوم ذي عذمراع إذا طال بالمستودع الأمد

ذي عذم appears to be a place name, provisionally rendered Dhū ʿAdham; its vocalization and location are uncertain. المستودع can mean either the person entrusted or the thing entrusted; the translation takes it as the person.

On the house (dār), line 4
Had Salmā suffered a loss like ours,it would have crumbled; yet ʿĀmir bears the loss.
ولو أن سلمى نالها مثل رزئنالهدت، ولكن تحمل الرزء عامر

Salmā probably denotes the mountain associated with Ṭayyiʾ, rather than a woman. ʿĀmir presumably denotes the tribe Banū ʿĀmir; neither identification is explicit in the verse.

On the house (dār), line 2
You reminded us of time’s changing fortunes and reversals,and showed us how calamities descend.
أذكرتنا دول الزمان وصرفهوأريتنا كيف الخطوب النزل

The unvocalized النزل is understood here as describing calamities that descend or befall; its precise vocalization and sense are uncertain.

On the house (dār), line 3
Then the land behind Jāsim, then the valleys of al-Ṣufr,the dwelling of tribes and white camels.
فقفا جاسم، فأودية الصفر مغى قبائل وهجان

The identification and vocalization of الصفر, provisionally transliterated al-Ṣufr, are uncertain. The name is split across the source hemistichs.

On the house (dār), line 5
May their mother be bereaved of them—and bereaved she was, the day they settled at Ḥārith al-Jawlān.
نكلت أمهموقد ثكلتهم يوم حلوا بحارث الجولان

Ḥārith al-Jawlān is treated as a place-name; its precise identification is uncertain.

On the house (dār), line 1
Night and day passed over Fahmibn ʿAmr, till they became like a field cut bare.
درج الليل والنهار على فهم بن عمرو فأصبحوا كالصريم

Fahm ibn ʿAmr appears to designate a clan collectively, accounting for the plural ‘they’; its precise identification is uncertain.

On the house (dār), line 1
A dwelling stirred your sorrows, as though it were—at Dhū Baqar or al-ʿUnābah—a gilded cloth.
وهاجت لك الأحزان دار كأنهابذي بقر أو بالعنابة مذهب

The precise object meant by مُذْهَب is uncertain: a gilded or gold-decorated article, provisionally rendered as 'gilded cloth.' The identification and vocalization of the place name العنابة are also uncertain.

On the house (dār), line 3
Once women with fair breasts dwelt there,like wild cows among the sand dunes.
وقد تحل بها بيض ترائبهاكأنها بين كثبان النقا البقر

«النقا» is taken here as a common noun referring to sandhills; it could instead be a place-name, al-Naqā.

On the house (dār), line 2
“Is it for a dwelling between Lūdhān and al-Naqāthat, this morning at al-Liwā, your eyes vie in shedding tears?”
أمن أجل دار بين لوذان والنقاغداة اللوى عيناك تبتدران؟

Lūdhān, al-Naqā, and al-Liwā are treated as place names, but their locations are uncertain. Al-Naqā and al-Liwā can also describe sandy terrain.

On the house (dār), line 1
Do you recognize the dwelling in the upper reaches of Dhū al-Qūr?It has vanished, save for buried ashes,
هل تعرف الدار بأعلى ذي القورقد درست غير رماد مكفور

Dhū al-Qūr is a place name whose location I could not identify.

On the house (dār), line 2
Dull-colored, windblown, rain-drenched—From the days when a wide-eyed woman was the joyful man's delight.
مكتئب اللون مراح ممطورأزمان عيناء سرور المسرور

I tentatively read مراح as describing ashes exposed to the wind. Without vocalization, it could also mean a resting place or livestock enclosure, though that fits the surrounding adjectives less naturally.

On the house (dār), line 1
My two friends of ʿAmr—may God pardon you bothand grant you ease in all your affairs.
خليلي من عمرو عفا الله عنكماولقاكما من كل أمركما يسرا

“Of ʿAmr” apparently indicates the two companions’ tribal affiliation; the particular group is unidentified.

On the house (dār), line 3
I looked at Armām—and what an hour it was!I cast a sidelong glance at its landmarks.
نظرت بأرمام، وأية ساعةنظرت إلى أعلامها نظرا شزرا

أرمام is taken as a place name, provisionally vocalized Armām; its identification is uncertain.

On the house (dār), line 1
O dwelling of Hind, effaced except for its hearthstones,between al-Ṭuwā, Ṣārāt, and its valley.
يا دار هند عفت إلا أثافيهابين الطوى فصارات فواديها

The identification and vocalization of the place names الطوى and صارات, rendered al-Ṭuwā and Ṣārāt, are uncertain.

On the house (dār), line 1
Has Sulaymā’s dwelling at al-Rawātik and al-ʿUrfendured the winds and the heavy, steady rains?
أدار سليمى بالرواتك والعرفأقامت على الأرواح والديم الوطف

Al-Rawātik and al-ʿUrf appear to be place names; their locations are unidentified.

On the house (dār), line 1
O dwelling of Mayya at al-ʿAlyāʾ, by al-Sanad,you stand deserted; long ages have passed over you.
يا دار مية بالعلياء فالسندأقوت وطال عليها سالف الأبد

Al-ʿAlyāʾ and al-Sanad may be place names or topographical descriptions: 'the high ground' and 'the slope.'

On the house (dār), line 4
And at al-Zurq are the deserted traces of Mayya's dwellings,swept by wind and rain for three years.
وبالزرق أطلال لمية أقفرتثلاثة أعوام تراح وتمطر

The vocalization of the place name الزرق, rendered al-Zurq, is uncertain.

On the house (dār), line 3
May it please you that I press my hand against my heart,and that my tears shimmer for fear of your departure.
ليهنك إمساكي بكفى على الحشاورقراق دمعي خيفة من زيالك

بكفى is read as بكفّي, “with my hand”; without vocalization, “with both my hands” is also possible.

On the house (dār), line 1
May we be your ransom—you, forsaken, who never reproached,and, excused for your desertion, were never blamed.
بنا أنت من مجفوة لم تعتبومعذورة في هجرها لم تؤنب

The unvocalized «لم تعتب» is ambiguous. I read it as “made no reproach”; other vocalizations could mean “was not reproached” or “was not appeased.”

On the house (dār), line 4
Do not remind him of al-Ḥimā, for its memoryis an inward anguish for the tormented, love-stricken man.
ألا لا تذكره الحمى إن ذكرهجوى باطن للمستهام المعذب

Al-Ḥimā is not securely identifiable here; the word can also mean protected pastureland rather than a specific place name.

On the house (dār), line 5
When we parted from al-Jizʿ, and drew far apart—the caravan’s eastward, upland-bound riders from those bound west—
ولما تزايلنا من الجزع وانتأىمشرق ركب مصعد عن مغرب

Al-Jizʿ is not securely identifiable here; the word can also denote a bend or stretch of a valley. The compressed phrase «مشرق ركب مصعد عن مغرب» is read as contrasting eastward, upland-bound riders with westward riders.

On the house (dār), line 1
Did you not know, O dwelling of Baljāʾ, that I—whether its surroundings are fertile or barren—
ألم تعلمي يا دار بلجاء أننيإذا أخصبت أو كان جدبا جنابها

Baljāʾ appears to be a woman's name, but I cannot identify her.

On the house (dār), line 1
O dwelling of Asmāʾ at al-Amthāl and al-Rajl,greetings to you, deserted campsite and ruined traces!
يا دار أسماء بالأمثال فالرجلحييت من دمنة قفر ومن طلل

Al-Amthāl and al-Rajl appear to be place names; their identification and precise vocalization are uncertain.

On the house (dār), line 1
O Laylā’s dwelling at Siqṭ al-Khall, you have been effaced,save for the thumām grass and the hearth.
يا دار ليلى بسقط الخل قد درستإلا الثمام، وإلا موقد النار

Siqṭ al-Khall is unidentified. The phrase may instead describe a location: 'at the edge of the sandy passage.'

On the house (dār), line 2
A dwelling at al-Barq cannot but stir my longing,and a home of hers between al-Ajāriʿ and al-Raḍm.
أبى منزل بالبرق إلا يهيجنيودار لها بين الأجارع والرضم

The locations are unidentified. Al-Ajāriʿ and al-Raḍm are provisionally treated as place names; they could instead describe sandy tracts and heaps of stones.

On the house (dār), line 1
I say to Jawwāb and Qays ibn ʿĀzib,while streaming tears have wet my eyelid:
أقول لجواب وقيس بن عازبوقد بل جفن العين ماء مسيلها

Jawwāb and Qays ibn ʿĀzib have not been securely identified.

On the house (dār), line 1
May God water a dwelling between the waters of Bāriqand Dhū Nakhb, of which only bare earth remains.
سقى الله دارا بين أمواه بارقوذي نخب لم يبق إلا صعيدها

The precise location of Dhū Nakhb and the vocalization of نخب are uncertain.

On the house (dār), line 2
The tent pegs of your dwelling did not leaf out at al-Liwāand Darah until they were watered with showers of tears.
وما أورقت أوتاد دارك باللوىودارة حتى أسقيت سبل الدمع

Darah is treated as a place name, but its precise location is uncertain.

On the house (dār), line 5
And when you settle at Dhū al-Arāk, with between usthe landmark of al-Murīb, Jawnah, and Taʿār,
وإذا حللت بذي الأراك ودونناعلم المريب وجونة وتعار

The locations al-Murīb, Jawnah, and Taʿār have not been securely identified here, and their vocalizations are tentative. علم المريب is taken as ‘the landmark of al-Murīb,’ though ʿAlam may form part of the place name.

On the house (dār), line 1
O dwelling of Mayya at al-Khalṣāʾ, then al-Jurd,may you be watered, though you stir even the faintest longing in the grief-stricken.
يا دار مية بالخلصاء فالجردسقيا، وإن هجت أدنى الشوق للكمد

The precise locations of al-Khalṣāʾ and al-Jurd are uncertain to me; the vocalization of al-Jurd is also uncertain.

On the house (dār), line 4
May God water Ḥuzwā with it, and let it drenchall the level land and hard ground facing al-Zurq.
أسقى الإله به حزوى، فجاد بهما قابل الزرق من سهل ومن جلد

Al-Zurq is a place-name here, but I cannot securely identify the location.

On the house (dār), line 2
O dwelling of love between al-Ṣarīmah and al-Liwā,Has love no aim but deep-seated, lingering anguish?
أدار الهوى بين الصريمة واللوىأما للهوى إلا رسيس الجوى قصد؟

The precise locations of al-Ṣarīmah and al-Liwā are uncertain.

On the house (dār), line 3
O her dwelling in al-Ḥazn! The journey to heris short, but terrors stand in the way.
فيا دارها بالحزن إن مزارهاقريب، ولكن دون ذلك أهوال

Al-Ḥazn may be a place name, or may simply mean rugged upland terrain. The pronoun in mazāruhā ('visiting her/it' or 'her/its place of visitation') could refer either to the woman or to her dwelling.

On the house (dār), line 1
If Nāʾil should ever dwell far away,then I fear nothing else that time may bring.
إذا نائل شطت بها الدار مرةفلست على شيء من الدهر أشفق

نائل appears to be the beloved’s name, Nāʾil, possibly a shortened form of Nāʾila; the reading and identification are uncertain.

On the house (dār), line 9
And a delightful season of pleasure in al-Maʿarra,at its Siyāth and on either side of its Harmās?
وزمان لهو بالمعرة مونقبسياثها، وبجانبي هرماسها

The identification and vocalization of سياث (rendered Siyāth) are uncertain. I also cannot securely identify the هرماس (Harmās) associated here with al-Maʿarra; the better-known river of that name is near Naṣībīn.

On the house (dār), line 10
The days when I said to a loving friend: pour mesome aged wine from its Ḥanāk or its Ḥās.
أيام قلت لذي المودة: سقنيمن خندريس حناكها أوحاسها

حناكها أوحاسها is read as ‘its Ḥanāk or its Ḥās,’ apparently naming wine-producing localities. The identification and vocalization of Ḥanāk are uncertain.

On the house (dār), line 1
May God water a home of mine, and a land I left,beside the two homes of Maʿqil and Yasār.
سقى الله دارا لي، وأرضا تركتهاإلى جنب داري معقل ويسار

Maʿqil and Yasār are unidentified. I read داري as the construct dual, ‘the two homes of’; the unvocalized text also permits ‘my home,’ yielding ‘beside my home are Maʿqil and Yasār.’

On the house (dār), line 2
Abū Mālik is its neighbor, and Ibn Burthun—what a pair of neighbors in abasement and disgrace!
أبو مالك جار لها، وابن برثنفيالك جاري ذلة وصغار"!

Abū Mālik and Ibn Burthun are unidentified; they may be animal sobriquets rather than people. The vocalization Burthun is uncertain.

On the house (dār), line 1
Greet the dwelling, deserted after long ages,a waste on the outskirts of upper Dhāt Imhād.
سلم على الدار أقوت بعد آبادقفرا بطارف أعلى ذات إمهاد

آباد is taken as the plural of أبد, 'ages.' Dhāt Imhād is treated as a place name, but its identification and vocalization are uncertain.

On the house (dār), line 3
In the wilderness, when it came into view, it seemed,from the valley of Dhāt al-Sanā, like tattered cloaks.
كأنها بالفيافي يوم مطلعهامن بطن ذات السنا أخلاق أبراد

The relation of يوم مطلعها ('when it appeared') to من بطن ذات السنا ('from the valley of Dhāt al-Sanā') is uncertain: the latter may locate the observer rather than the ruins. Dhāt al-Sanā has not been identified.

On the house (bayt), line 2
At the abode of a fair, noble man from the two branches of Luʾayy ibn Ghālib,among the highest when their pedigrees are examined.
بأبيض من فرعي لوي بن غالبإذا حصلت أنسابها في الذوائب

The two branches of Luʾayy ibn Ghālib are not identified. The syntax of the second hemistich is compressed; “among the highest” is taken as describing the praised man’s genealogical standing.

On the house (bayt), line 3
He refuses to submit to injustice and delights in generosity;his two grandfathers stood amid the branches of the noblest.
أبي لأخذ الضيم يرتاح للندىتوسط جداه فروع الأطايب

جداه is read as جدّاه, “his two grandfathers.” Without vocalization it could also mean “his bounty,” but the genealogical imagery favors the former reading.

On the house (bayt), line 1
Help me weep, you two, with streaming tears,With tears poured forth in abundance.
أسعداني بعبرة أسرابمن دموع كثيرة التسكاب

The unusual expression «عبرة أسراب» is understood as streaming tears; the precise form and vocalization of «أسراب» are uncertain.

On the house (bayt), line 2
The people of al-Ḥaṣāb have left meConsumed with longing, devoted to the people of al-Ḥaṣāb.
إن أهل الحصاب قد تركونيموزعا مولعا بأهل الحصاب

The precise identification and vocalization of «الحصاب», provisionally transliterated al-Ḥaṣāb, are uncertain.

On the house (bayt), line 1
Ah, to the lofty dwellings by al-Liwā—Liwā al-Raml—will souls ever return?
ألا هل إلى أبيات شمخ إلى اللوىلوى الرمل يوما للنفوس معاد؟

The unvocalized شمخ is uncertain: translated here as “lofty,” it could instead be a proper name, Shamkh, giving “the dwellings of Shamkh.”

On the house (bayt), line 4
May rain water al-Ṣafarāt as long as he liesthere, and may its promising clouds drench the people of Shawl.
سقى الصفرات الغيث ما دام ثاويابهن، وجادت أهل شول مخايله

Al-Ṣafarāt and Shawl are provisionally treated as place names; their identification and vocalization are uncertain. أهل شول could alternatively mean 'owners of dry she-camels.'

On the house (bayt), line 1
By your life, that house at al-Ẓāhir—I passed without stopping there—fills me with longing.
لعمرك إن البيت بالظاهر الذيمررت فلم ألمم به لي شائق

Al-Ẓāhir is taken as a place-name; its location is uncertain.

On the house (bayt), line 3
At al-Jarʿ, in upper al-Junayna, stands a dwelling,wide in expanse, yet there my breast is constricted.
وبالجرع من أعلى الجنينة منزلفسيح شحا صدري به متضايق

Al-Junayna is not securely identified. Al-Jarʿ may be a place-name or a description meaning sandy ground.

On the house (bayt), line 1
O you two tents at al-Ajraʿ, whoselower open ground holds ghaḍā shrubs and a sand dune!
ألا أيها البيتان بالأجرع الذيبأسفل مفضاه غضى وكثيب

Al-Ajraʿ may be a place name or simply a description of sandy ground; its location is unidentified.

On the house (bayt), line 3
Do you weep for Lubnā, when you yourself left her,though at al-Malā you had the power to keep her?
أتبكي على لبنى وأنت تركتهاوأنت عليها بالملا كنت تقدر

بالملا is uncertain. It is provisionally treated as the place-name al-Malā, whose location here is unidentified; it might instead represent بالملأ, 'before the assembly' or 'in public.' 'Had the power to keep her' interprets the more literal 'had power over her.'

On the house (bayt), line 4
Even if she had what Ibn Bajra possessesof wine, she would not moisten my palate with a single measure.
ولو أن ما عند ابن بجرة عندهامن الخمر لم تبلل لهاتي بناطل

Ibn Bajra is apparently associated with a supply of wine, but his identity and the vocalization of his name are uncertain.

On the house (bayt), line 1
I lodged with the clan of Makhul; their guestis like one encamped beyond all human sight and hearing.
نزلت في آل مكحول، وضيفهمكنازل بين سمع الأرض والبصر

The clan of Makhul is unidentified.

On the house (bayt), line 1
You grew indifferent at Aʿshāsh, though you could scarcely do so,and no longer recognized in Ḥadrāʾ what you once knew.
عزفت بأعشاش وما كدت تعزفوأنكرت من حدراء ما كنت تعرف

Aʿshāsh is taken as a place-name; its location is uncertain.

On the house (bayt), line 1
I passed by the tents of Kās, and down streamedthe tears of my eyes, while the winds swayed them.
مررت على أبيات كاس فأسبلتمدامع عيني، والرياح تميلها

Kās (كاس) appears to be a personal or place name, but I cannot identify it or confirm its vocalization.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 4
Did I not keep company with ʿAmr and Mālik,and Adham, who went forth among horsemen or men on foot?
ألم أك قد صاحبت عمرا ومالكاوأدهم يغدو في فوارس أو رجل؟

ʿAmr, Mālik, and Adham cannot be securely identified from this passage. رجل is read as a collective meaning ‘men on foot,’ contrasted with horsemen.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 5
I kept company with Shaybān and with Ḍābiʾ,and the proud, tall Banū Shibl were my companions.
وصاحبت شيبانا وصاحبت ضابئاوصاحبني الشم الطوال بنو شبل

Shaybān, Ḍābiʾ, and the Banū Shibl cannot be securely identified from this passage.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
I wept for Sharīk in al-Ghawār, and for Aswad,and Dhū al-ʿAlaq, until no moisture remained in my eyes.
بكيت شريكا في الغوار، وأسوداوذو العلق حتى ما بعيني من بلل

Al-Ghawār is provisionally treated as a place name; I cannot identify it securely, and الغوار may instead refer to raiding. ذو العلق appears to be a personal epithet, but its expected accusative form here would be ذا العلق.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
Since Muḍarris and Mughallis are gone, I have becomea target on open ground for whoever would shoot at me.
أصبحت بعد مضرس ومغلسغرضا بصردحة لمن راماني

Muḍarris and Mughallis appear to be personal names, but their identities and exact vocalization are uncertain.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 3
Is it true that I shall never meet Ziyād, nor seeQinān leading the cavalry, his locks disheveled?
أجدى لن ألقى زيادا، ولا أرىقنانا يقود الخيل شعثا ذوائبه

أجدى appears to represent أجِدّي, an interrogative expression meaning approximately 'Is it really true?' The transmitted spelling is uncertain. The unvocalized personal name قنان is provisionally read Qinān.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 2
men among my kinsfolk who have died,men of Khidhām, the great leaders.
من رجال من الأقارب فادوامن خذام، هم الرؤوس العظام

خذام appears to name a kinship group; its identification and vocalization are uncertain. Khidhām is provisional.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 7
Rather, we have journeyed through them with unyielding souls,laden with what they cannot bear, yet bearing it.
ولكن رحلناها نفوسا أبيةتحمل ما لا تستطيع فتحمل

The unvocalized تحمل ... فتحمل is read here as تُحَمَّل ... فتَحْمِل: 'are laden ... yet bear.' Other vocalizations are possible.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
I bore patiently, seeking reward, the loss of Khuwaylidand of Rizam—for souls grow attached to one another.
صبرت ابتغاء الأجر بعد خويلدوبعد رزام والنفوس توالف

Khuwaylid and Rizam have not been identified; the vocalization of رزام as Rizam is uncertain.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 2
And of the young man Fajr and Layth, who followed one another in death;after the beloved companion, only acquaintances remained.
وبعد الفتى فجر وليث تتابعافلم يبقى بعد الإلف إلا المعارف

فجر is taken as the personal name Fajr, but this reading is uncertain. Neither Fajr nor Layth has been identified.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
Who has seen Ibn Arwā’s caravan on the expanseof the desert, its camel-drivers hurrying?
من رأى العير لابن أروى على ظهر المروري حداتهن عجال

I take المروري as a spelling of المَرَوْرَى, meaning open deserts or wilderness, rather than a place name. Ibn Arwā may be ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, whose mother was Arwā, but the identification is uncertain.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 2
Heading upland, while the house—the house of Abū Wahb—stands empty, the north wind blowing through it.
مصعدات، والبيت بيت أبي وهب خلاء تهب فيه الشمال

Abū Wahb may be al-Walīd ibn ʿUqba, an associate of the poet, but this identification is not certain.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 5
After all that you know, O Umm Zayd—among them we once had honor and splendor:
بعد ما تعلمين يا أم زيدكان فيهم عز لنا وجمال

Umm Zayd is unidentified. The syntax of بعد ما تعلمين is compressed; I take it as referring back to their passing after the former circumstances known to her.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 5
As though my old mother had borne only one son,though she died at Dhāt al-Sharā no barren woman.
كأن عجوزي لم تلد غير واحدوماتت بذات الشرى غير عقيم

Dhāt al-Sharā (ذات الشرى) is an unidentified place; its vocalization is uncertain.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
Had my people been like the people of ʿAbāʿiband their brothers, my riding camels would not have been driven off unjustly.
ولو أن قومي مثل قوم عباعبوإخوتهم ما استيق ظلما ركائبي

ʿAbāʿib (عباعب) is unidentified; the vocalization of the name is uncertain.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
Between al-Ḥarīsh and Tall Maḥrā lie buriedhorsemen of Nimārah, never wavering.
ثوى بين الحريش وتل محرىفوارس من نمارة غير ميل

The precise identification and vocalization of al-Ḥarīsh and Tall Maḥrā are uncertain. Nimārah appears to be a tribal name, but its identification here is uncertain.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 2
Alas for those slain at al-Nibāj! Theywere the summits and the firmly rooted mountains.
لهفي على قتلى النباج فإنهمكانوا الذرى ورواسي الأعلام

I could not identify the particular battle or killings at al-Nibāj to which this refers.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
After Abū Ḥiṣn, Ḥuṣayn, and Mālik and ʿAbda, shall I weep for the dead and grieve?
أبعد أبي حصن حصين، ومالك وعبدة، أبكى الهالكين وأجزع

I take Ḥuṣayn as an appositive identifying Abū Ḥiṣn. The individuals mentioned are not securely identified, and the unvocalized name عبدة is provisionally rendered ʿAbda.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 2
Though Mālik was left where he lay,there are examples to console me, if such consolation can help:
لئن مالك خلي على مكانهلفي أسوة إن كان ينفعني الأسى

خلي على مكانه is ambiguous without vocalization. I have provisionally read it as “was left where he lay”; an active reading, possibly with عليّ rather than على, could mean that Mālik left his place vacant for the speaker. The syntax of لفي أسوة with the following line is also uncertain. الأسى is taken here as أُسَى, “consoling examples,” rather than أَسَى, “grief.”

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
Who will deal with disputants when their quarrel grows fierceafter Ibn Saʿd—and who will care for the lean, long-necked steeds?
من للخصوم إذا جد الخصام بهمبعد ابن سعد، ومن للضمر القود

Ibn Saʿd cannot be securely identified from this extract. The phrase asking who will be there for the steeds leaves his precise role unstated; “care for” is interpretive.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 3
Oh, my grief for one dead at Naʿmān—for the young man!And my grief for one dead at Qaws al-Maʿāqil!
فلهفي على ميت بنعمان للفتىولهفي على ميت بقوس المعاقل

Naʿmān is probably the valley near Mecca. I cannot securely identify قوس المعاقل; it is provisionally treated as the place-name Qaws al-Maʿāqil, though المعاقل may instead describe its strongholds.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
After Zirr’s sons and after Ibn Jandal,and ʿAmr, can I hope to enjoy life at ease?
أبعد بني زر وبعد ابن جندلوعمرو، أرجى لذة العيش في خفض

Ibn Jandal and ʿAmr could not be identified; the vocalization of Jandal is uncertain.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 2
I said, “Should I weep for ʿAbd Allah, or for the oneon al-Sharaf al-Aʿlā, slain by Abū Bakr?
فقلت: أعبد الله أبكي، أم الذيعلى الشرف الأعلى، قتيل أبي بكر؟

Al-Sharaf al-Aʿlā may be a place-name or simply mean “the highest ridge.” Abū Bakr is not securely identified here; the name may designate a clan rather than an individual.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 3
And ʿAbd Yaghūth—or my companion Mālik?Grievous is the loss: heaping grave upon grave.
وعبد يغوث أم نديمي مالكاوعز المصاب حثو قبر على قبر

Mālik, described as the poet’s companion, is not securely identified.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 2
Do you not know that I am alone at Samʿān,with no loved one there but you two?
ألم تعلما أني بسمعان مفردومالي فيه من حبيب سواكما؟

The location سمعان, provisionally transliterated Samʿān, is unidentified; its vocalization is uncertain.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 2
Do you not know that I have no brother in Rāwand,nor any drinking companion in Jazāq besides you two?
أم تعلما مالي براوند من أخولا بجزاق من نديم سواكما

The verse names جزاق (provisionally vocalized Jazāq), while the introduction gives حزاق (Ḥazāq). The correct spelling and identification are uncertain; the verse's spelling is retained. Rāwand's precise location is also uncertain.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
We stood at a grave in Dasm, and it stirred our griefand reminded us of life when it was kind to us.
وقفنا على قبر بدسم فهاجناوذكرنا بالعيش إذ هو مصحب

دسم is treated as a place name and provisionally vocalized Dasm; its precise vocalization and location are uncertain.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 2
The people of al-Ḥiṣāb have left meconsumed with longing, enthralled by the people of al-Ḥiṣāb.
إن أهل الحصاب قد تركونيموزعا مولعا بأهل الحصاب

الحصاب is treated as the place-name al-Ḥiṣāb, apparently associated with the Meccan pilgrimage grounds; its precise identification and vocalization are uncertain.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
Bereft was their mother! What fell with them the day they were slainat Ḥasmān—what pillars of glory!
هوت أمهم ماذا بهم يوم صرعوابحسمان من أسباب مجد تهدما

The place حسمان is unidentified here; the vocalization Ḥasmān is uncertain.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
May God curse an age whose evil is nearer than its good,and the fortune that took Ṣayfī away after Maʿbad.
لحى الله دهرا شره دون خيرهوجدا بصيفي نأى بعد معبد

Ṣayfī and Maʿbad appear to be deceased companions; I cannot identify them more precisely.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
Desolate now are the places where my people dwelt:the spacious-walled homes, their uplands and plains.
أصبحت من حلول قومي وحشارحب الجدر جلسها فالبطاح

The phrase رحب الجدر is uncertain. I have provisionally understood it as 'spacious-walled homes'; it may instead contain a place-name.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
Have you not yet ceased longing for Laylā, though your life has passed,and al-Mawārij and al-Ḥaḍr lie desolate without her?
ألم تسل عن ليلى وقد ذهب العمروقد أوحشت منها الموارج والحضر

Al-Mawārij and al-Ḥaḍr appear to be place names, but their locations are uncertain; the vocalization of al-Ḥaḍr is provisional.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 2
There stirred my longing for her, on the sands of Furūʿ,and the sandy flats of Dhū al-Lahbāʾ, a deserted dwelling.
وقد هاجني منها بوعساء فروعفأجراع ذي اللهباء منزلة قفر

Furūʿ and Dhū al-Lahbāʾ appear to be place names whose locations I cannot identify. The vocalization of Furūʿ is uncertain.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
Who has seen a lightning cloud that I spent the night watching,lavishing rain upon al-Ḥarra al-Sawdāʾ and the valley?
يا من رأى بارقا قد بت أرمقهجودا، على الحرة السوداء والوادي

Al-Ḥarra al-Sawdāʾ means 'the black lava field'; it may be a description rather than a fixed place-name. I cannot identify the location.

One reading chosen among several

The Arabic allows more than one sense, usually because it is unvocalized, and the translator chose one.

On encampments (manāzil), line 2
Where are those I once knew within you,through whom time dealt harm and benefit?
أين الذين عهدتهم بك مرةكان الزمان بهم يضر وينفع

The force of بهم is ambiguous: 'through whom' suggests that these people were agents of harm and benefit; alternatively, the phrase may indicate that they themselves experienced time's harm and benefit.

On encampments (manāzil), line 3
There is no hope of a return that would reunitetheir scattered company, until the Gathering brings them together.
لا يرتجى لهم إياب جامعلشتاتهم حتى يضم المجمع

I understand al-majmaʿ (“the gathering” or “place of assembly”) as the gathering at the Resurrection, though this is not explicitly stated.

On encampments (manāzil), line 2
Generosity settled in your gathering-place, and the winds breatheda faint breath in your courtyard.
أرسى بناديك الندى وتنفستنفسا بعقوتك الرياح ضعيفا

الندى can mean either generosity or dew. I have chosen generosity, in keeping with the gathering-place and the imagery of hospitality in line 4.

On encampments (manāzil), line 4
Though we see it settling down within you—calamity, your guest—it has indeed found a host.
ولئن نرى بك ملقيا أجرانهضيف الخطوب، لقد أصاب مضيفا

ملقيا أجرانه appears to evoke a camel laying its neck on the ground to settle down. The form أجرانه is unusual; I have taken it as a plural referring to necks and rendered the apparent sense.

On encampments (manāzil), line 1
Come to your senses: my family has been ravagedby deadly doom and the onslaught of calamities.
فيء إليك، فقد تخون أسرتيحتف الردى وتحامل النكبات

فيء إليك is unusual as printed. The translation assumes فِئْ إليك, an injunction to return to oneself or recover one's composure.

On encampments (manāzil), line 5
Every place once theirs lies desolate,and every encampment of theirs is buried.
فكل عهد لهم محيلوكل ربع لهم دفين

عهد is taken here as a formerly familiar abode, with محيل meaning altered or desolate. عهد can also mean a bond or remembered acquaintance, so the first hemistich remains somewhat ambiguous.

On encampments (manāzil), line 1
O company of loved ones—their dwellings have now become graves.
يا معشر الأحباب قدأضحت منازلهم قبورا

The Arabic addresses the loved ones directly, then refers to 'their dwellings' in the third person; this shift is retained.

On encampments (manāzil), line 2
I was the youngest; if only Ihad not been left to grow old after them.
كنت الصغير فليتنيلم أدع بعدهم كبيرا

The unvowelled أدع is read here as 'be left,' though 'be called' is also possible. الصغير and كبيرا may contrast the youngest with the eldest, rather than youth with old age.

On encampments (manāzil), line 4
Once I had a love within you;time changed it, and never wearied.
قد كان لي فيك هوى مرةغيره الدهر وما ملا

وما ملا is read as وما مَلَّا ('and did not weary'), with a rhyme-lengthening final alif. The translation takes 'time' as its subject, though the reference is not entirely certain.

On encampments (manāzil), line 3
I see people returning to their dwellings and rain-watered lands,but the wanderers of Kaʿb ibn ʿAmr do not return.
أرى الناس راعوا للديار وللحياوكعب بن عمرو لا يريع شريدها

الحيا literally means rain; 'rain-watered lands' takes it as referring to places offering pasture after rainfall.

On encampments (manāzil), line 2
A burly-armed man set upon them, as thoughtime had kindled between them the war of Wāʾil.
تصدى لها عبل الذراع، كأنماجنى الدهر فيما بينهم حرب وائل

The “war of Wāʾil” probably refers to the Basus War between Bakr and Taghlib, tribes descended from Wāʾil. The comparison apparently casts the man and the stones as hereditary enemies.

On encampments (manāzil), line 4
For I had known that parting has a cryover the tribe, on a day cruel to your soul.
فقد كنت أدرى أن للبين صيحةعلى الحي في يوم لنفسك ضائم

I read أدرى as أدري, ‘I knew,’ giving a shift from second-person address to first-person speech. As written, it could instead be أدرى, ‘better aware,’ allowing ‘you knew better.’

On encampments (manāzil), line 3
How lovely were the days when her people encampedat Dhāt al-Ghaḍā, and the tribe thronged the dwelling-place!
فيا حبذا أيام يحتل أهلهابذات الغضا والحي في الدار آهل

The feminine pronoun in أهلها ('her/its people') has no explicit antecedent. It may refer to a beloved, as translated, or to an abode.

On encampments (manāzil), line 3
How dear to me is that valley bend as a dwelling,those acacias as acacias, those camel-watering grounds as watering grounds!
أحبب إلي بذاك الجزع منزلةبالطلح طلحا وبالأعطان أعطانا

The repeated nouns in the second hemistich are syntactically compressed. I take them as continuing the exclamation, specifying the acacias and camel-watering grounds as further objects of affection.

On encampments (manāzil), line 5
so that gloating men might see my firmness,while I hold that grief in check with restraint and modesty.
ليرى الرجال الشامتون صلابتيوأكف ذاك بعفة وحياء

‘That grief’ interprets ذاك (‘that’) as referring to the mourning or distress described earlier; its precise referent is not explicit.

On encampments (manāzil), line 2
Dwellings at whose sight no eye escaped unharmed,nor, since the parting, has any well of tears there filled again.
منازل لم تسلم عليهن مقلةولا جم بعد البين فيهن مدمع

The phrase «ولا جم ... مدمع» is ambiguous. I take جم to mean ‘filled again,’ with مدمع as a source or well of tears, continually drained by weeping. A sense closer to ‘no tearful eye found rest’ may also be intended.

On encampments (manāzil), line 3
You have taken gazelles and wide-eyed wild cattlein place of bashful, noble women.
استبدلت بالظباء والبقر العين خلاف العقائل الخرد

The construction استبدلت بالظباء ... خلاف العقائل is unusual: the preposition would normally mark what was relinquished. The translation follows the apparent sense that wild animals have replaced the women.

On encampments (manāzil), line 3
And at Dārat al-Salam, for which I yearned,Are traces of dwellings whose doves keep making us weep.
وبدارة السلم التي شوقتهادمن يظل حمامها يبكينا

شوقتها is interpreted as passive شُوِّقْتُها, ‘I was made to yearn for it.’ The unvocalized form is ambiguous. يبكينا is read as يُبكينا, ‘makes us weep,’ though ‘weeps for us’ is also possible.

On encampments (manāzil), line 3
If I weep, I shall surely weep from longing;and if I endure, I shall surely endure with fortitude.
فلئن بكيت لأبكين صبابةولئن صبرت لأصبرن جليدا

The unvocalized بكيت and صبرت can mean either 'I wept/endured' or 'you wept/endured.' Both are taken here as first person.

On encampments (manāzil), line 4
It fell to ruin, emptied of human company, asthe sanctuaries of long-vanished peoples lay deserted.
بادت وأقوت من الإنيس كماأقوت محاريب دارس الأمم

The unusual expression دارس الأمم is taken to mean peoples or nations that have long vanished.

On encampments (manāzil), line 2
I say, “There is a mole on his cheek,” when I mention him,for fear of the watcher, though there is no mole on his cheek.
أقول: بالخد خال حين أذكرهخوف الرقيب، وما بالخد من خال

The referent of 'him' in أذكره is not explicit; I take it to be the beloved. The Arabic says simply 'the cheek,' without an explicit possessive.

On encampments (manāzil), line 2
You will learn, if distant exile carries them far away,and they depart with Laylā, that your reason will depart,
ستعمل إن شطت بهم غربة النوىوزالوا بليلي أن لبك زائل

ستعمل ('you will act/work') appears to be a transposition error for ستعلم ('you will learn'). بليلي is read as بليلى ('with Laylā').

On encampments (manāzil), line 1
You tirelessly cover the stages, away from your beloved,yet keep weeping for him with streaming tears.
تطوى المنازل عن حبيبك دائباوتظل تبكيه بدمع ساجم

Read تطوى as تطوي, 'you traverse,' rather than the passive 'are traversed'; the following second-person address supports this reading.

On encampments (manāzil), line 2
They will admonish you without a word, for they have seenhow their hopes and death wrestle with one another.
تخبرك وعظا بلا لفظ فقد نظرتآمالهم والمنايا كيف تصطرع

The unvocalized نظرت can mean either 'they [the dwellings] have seen' or 'you have seen.' The translation takes the dwellings as its subject.

On encampments (manāzil), line 4
To them I send a greeting whose fragrancewafts abroad like the praise of them today.
فعليهم مني سلام نشرهمتضوع كثنائهم في الحاضر

في الحاضر is taken to mean 'in the present,' hence 'today'; it could also mean 'among those present.'

On encampments (manāzil), line 1
May your haunts—hills and dwellings—be greetedby clouds passing in the night, with every pouring shower.
حيي ربوعك من ربى ومنازلساري الغمام بكل هام هامل

The opening حيي appears to stand for حيّا, ‘may ... greet,’ with the night-traveling clouds as its delayed subject.

On encampments (manāzil), line 6
I spent them lavishly, and here I standon barren ground, weeping with a parched eyelid.
أنفقته سرفا وهأنا ماثلفي ماحل أبكى بجفن ما حل

The final ما حل is likewise read as ماحل, ‘parched,’ echoing the same word earlier in the hemistich for barren ground.

On encampments (manāzil), line 1
May my tears dry up at the dwellings, and may I regainmy patience, and may sleep that fled return to me,
غاضت دموعي في المنازل وارعوىصبري، وراجعني الرقاد النافر

The expression ارعوى صبري is unusual: ارعوى ordinarily means 'desisted' or 'came to his senses.' I understand it here as patience returning or reasserting itself. The line is read as an imprecation conditional on 'if I do not' in line 2.

On encampments (manāzil), line 2
Pour out your tears upon their soil,until blood mingles with them.
فاسفح دموعك في ثراها أو يمازجها الدم

I take أو here in the sense of 'until'; it could also be read literally as 'or,' giving 'or let blood mingle with them.'

On encampments (manāzil), line 5
O dwelling, I owe you all my eye can give;it is no disgrace to me if the rain clouds withhold their rain.
على يا دار جهد عيني وماعلى عار أن تبخل الديم

Both occurrences of على are read as عليّ ('upon me'), which fits the sense; the printed spelling is irregular.

On encampments (manāzil), line 3
She saw a gray hair, not yet conspicuous at my temples,and every veiled hint proclaimed estrangement outright.
رأت شيبة ما صرحت لعوارضيفصرح بالهجران كل معرض

كل معرض is read as referring to veiled hints or indirect expressions, in contrast with صرح, ‘spoke openly.’ The unvocalized wording could instead refer to someone speaking indirectly or turning away.

On encampments (manāzil), line 2
And Tūḍiḥ and al-Miqrāt—its traces have not vanished,Thanks to what the south and north winds have woven over them.
فتوضح، فالمقراة لم يعف رسمهالما نسجته من جنوب وشمأل

The relation expressed by «لما نسجته» is ambiguous. I take it causally: the winds alternately cover and uncover the traces, preserving them. It can also be understood as saying that the traces have survived despite the winds’ weaving.

On encampments (manāzil), line 4
My cure would be a tear, if I could shed it;But can weeping at an effaced trace avail?
وإن شفائي عبرة لو سفحتهافهل عند رسم دارس من معول؟

«معول» can signify weeping or a place for weeping, but also a source of reliance or refuge. The translation reflects the possible overlap between lamentation and the relief sought from it.

On encampments (manāzil), line 2
Ruins that bent the heart’s resolve; scatteredamong them were the eye’s tears in every direction.
دمن لوت عزم الفؤاد ومزقتفيها دموع العين كل ممزق

I read ومزقت as passive, 'were scattered,' with 'the eye’s tears' as its subject. The unvocalized text also permits an active reading, though its object would then be implicit.

On encampments (manāzil), line 1
Sickness lies between me and those languid eyes,and torment between me and those sweet teeth.
سقم دون أعين ذات سقموعذاب دون الثنايا العذاب

The precise force of دون is ambiguous. I take sickness and torment as intervening between the speaker and the beloved’s eyes and teeth; “me” is implicit rather than expressed.

On encampments (manāzil), line 2
May the spring rains fall upon you both in succession!Have you no recollection of al-Mālikiyya?
تتابع أنواء الربيع عليكماأمالكما بالمالكية من عهد؟

Al-Mālikiyya may designate a woman belonging to the tribe of Mālik rather than a place. The question could also mean ‘Have you any recent knowledge of the Mālikī woman?’

On encampments (manāzil), line 1
As though Saʿdā had never lived among the tribes of Ghayqa,and no dwellings of Laylā had ever been seen among them;
كأن لم تكن سعدى بأحياء غيقةولم ترى من ليلى بهن منازل

The written form «لم ترى» is irregular after «لم». I have understood it as passive «لم تُرَ», ‘had not been seen’; an active reading, ‘you had not seen’, is also possible.

On encampments (manāzil), line 2
I know full well—and not from anyone’s report—
لقد علمتوما أخبرت عن أحد

The supplied lines 2–3 appear to be a single bayt divided incorrectly: لقد علمت وما أخبرت عن أحد / أن الهوى بنقا البشرين معتادي. The supplied divisions have been preserved.

On encampments (manāzil), line 6
My chastity restrains me without need of fear;your modesty guards you without need of a watcher.
عفافي من دون التقية زاجروصونك من دون الرقيب رقيب

Ṣawnuka, translated as “your modesty,” can mean your guarding of your own honor or the speaker’s safeguarding of you; the translation takes the former.

On encampments (manāzil), line 4
I stirred with longing, and my heart said: “Are her peopleonly a few short nights away from those she once dwelt beside?”
طربت، وقال القلب: هل دون أهلهالمن جاورت إلا ليال قلائل؟

The construction لمن جاورت is ambiguous. The translation reads جاورت as “she dwelt beside” and takes the phrase to mean “for those whose neighbor she once was.”

On encampments (manāzil), line 2
I kept showing them to my companions; once I would seetheir people there, both young and gray-haired,
ظللت أرائيها صحابي، وقد أرىبها أهلها من بين غر وأشيبا

The wording «من بين غر وأشيبا» is grammatically irregular as transmitted, particularly the accusative-looking «أشيبا» after «بين». The translation takes it as a contrast between youthful and gray-haired inhabitants; «غر» could also suggest fair or radiant faces.

On encampments (manāzil), line 3
Leave me, you two—love’s summoner from her landis never heedless when Kharqāʾ is far from me.
دعاني، وما داعي الهوى من بلادهاإذا ما نأت خرقاء عني بغافل

I read دعاني as the dual imperative, “leave me, you two,” addressed to the two companions. The unvocalized text also permits “he/it called me,” with an implied subject.

On encampments (manāzil), line 1
O you, time-worn dwelling, fare well!May the cloud-darkened morning’s downpour water you.
ألا أيهذا المنزل الدارس اسلموأسقيت صوب الباكر المتغيم

The referent of الباكر المتغيم is implicit; I take it as the cloud-darkened early morning, though an early-arriving raincloud may be intended.

On encampments (manāzil), line 2
He asks the dwellings about them; upon al-Liwālie faded traces that, if you question them, will not answer.
يسل المنازل عنهم، وعلى اللوىدمن دوارس إن تسل لم تخبر

يسل is understood as يسأل ('he asks'), apparently with the hamza omitted for meter.

On encampments (manāzil), line 3
And such anguish for its people—were I to complain of itto the dwelling, its rocks would soften, solid though they are.
ومن لوعة من أهله لو شكوتهاإليه للانت وهي صم جلامده

The opening wa-min lawʿatin ('and of/from anguish') is grammatically elliptical. I have rendered it as an expression of intense grief for the departed inhabitants.

On encampments (manāzil), line 4
He lingered, seeking a scattered companyof Laylā’s kin, a band still disunited.
أقام ينشد شملا غير متفقمن آل ليلى، وشعبا غير ملتئم

شعبا غير ملتئم is taken as ‘a band still disunited.’ شعب can also mean a rift, allowing the alternative ‘a rift still unhealed.’

On encampments (manāzil), line 2
We turned aside: some were lovelorn, in pouring out their tearswell practiced; others made an effort, still learning.
عجنا فمن صب بصب دموعهدرب، ومن متعمل متعلم

متعمل may suggest someone forcing or affecting tears, in contrast to the practiced lover; here rendered as someone making an effort.

On encampments (manāzil), line 3
Set out this evening on a journey to be remembered:if they die, we die; if they live, we live.
روحوا العشية روحة مذكورةإن متن متن، وإن حيين حيينا

The second متن appears to be missing a final alif. The translation assumes متنا, ‘we die,’ parallel to حيينا, ‘we live’; as printed, متن means ‘they [feminine plural] die.’

On encampments (manāzil), line 2
So I deliberately refrained from revealing her secret,and she too deliberately refrained from revealing it.
فحدت عن الإظهار عمد السرهاوحادت عن الإظهار أيضا على عمد

The wording «عمد السرها» appears incorrectly spaced. I read it as «عمدًا لسرّها», taking «لسرّها» with «الإظهار»: ‘deliberately refrained from revealing her secret.’

On encampments (manāzil), line 3
On nights when she captivated you with a mouth of sharp-edged teeth,their lustre like dew-moistened chamomile blossoms.
ليالي تستبيك بذي غروبيشبه ظلمه خضل الأقاح

ذي غروب is understood as an implied mouth with sharp-edged teeth. ظلمه can denote the teeth’s lustre or their moisture; خضل الأقاح is taken as dew-moistened chamomile blossoms, though the comparison may refer specifically to their moisture.

On dwellings (diyār), line 2
Once we would see their gathering at the valley bend—a great assembly—and the kneeling-ground of a vast camel herd.
ولقد نرى بالجزع منهم مجلساضخما، ومبرك جامل قمقام

الجزع is translated as 'the valley bend,' but it could instead designate a particular locality, al-Jizʿ.

On dwellings (diyār), line 4
So leave off weeping over the dwellings, foryour eyes have fulfilled their vow of streaming tears.
فاترك بكاءك في الديار فقد قضتعيناك نحبهما من التسجام

قضت عيناك نحبهما literally says that the eyes have 'fulfilled their vow.' The idiom commonly means 'met their death,' and may here portray the eyes as spent or destroyed by weeping.

On dwellings (diyār), line 1
And whenever my longing growsfor you, and my beating heart catches fire,
وإني كلما زاد التياحيإليك وأضرم القلب الخفوق

التياحي is an unusual form, understood here as “my longing.” وأضرم القلب الخفوق may mean either “my beating heart catches fire” or “the fluttering sets my heart ablaze.”

On dwellings (diyār), line 2
And shall I ever see those dwellings wheremy drinking companions once were, where I myself used to be?
وهل أرين تلك الديار التي بهانداماي قدما حيث كنت أراني؟

The final phrase literally means 'where I used to see myself'; it is rendered here as 'where I myself used to be.'

On dwellings (diyār), line 2
They have stirred sorrow; from them you havetoday only anguish and remembrance.
أسفا هيجت فمالك منها اليوم إلا تفجع وإدكار

The unvocalized هيجت is ambiguous: I read it as 'they [the dwellings] have stirred,' but it could also address someone: 'you have stirred.'

On dwellings (diyār), line 1
Ah, dwellings of the tribe, between Muḥajjarand the edge of al-Qumrī, as though unchanged!
ألا يا ديار الحي بين محجرإلى جانب القمري كأنه لم تغير

The wording كأنه لم تغير appears grammatically damaged: the pronoun and verb do not clearly agree with ديار. 'As though unchanged' renders the likely sense. The construction بين ... إلى ('between ... to') is also irregular.

On dwellings (diyār), line 2
You stood there, yet you satisfy no longing,nor does despair cure the yearning of one who remembers.
وقفت بها لا أنت قاض لبانةولا اليأس يشفي حاجة المتذكر

The unvocalized وقفت can mean 'I stood' or 'you stood.' The latter is adopted to agree with the following أنت; the former would involve a shift into self-address.

On dwellings (diyār), line 2
I once lived under the protection of a cherished neighbor;in Arbad I lost a helpful protector.
وقد كنت في أكناف جار مضنةففارقني جار بأربد نافع

The construction «جار بأربد نافع» is unusual. I take Arbad to be the cherished neighbor and protector whose loss is lamented.

On dwellings (diyār), line 6
The tribe's movements brought us together there for a year,taking pleasure in our concealed secret.
جمعتنا بها نوى الحي حولانتلهى بسرنا المكتوم

نوى الحي can refer to the tribe's intended destination or journey; 'the tribe's movements' leaves this distinction open.

On dwellings (diyār), line 2
A deluded man rejoices in the flourishing of dwellings,yet their flourishing draws them nearer to their ruin.
يسر بعمران الديار مضللوعمرانها تدنو بها من خرابها

The grammar of وعمرانها تدنو بها is irregular: the feminine verb تدنو does not agree with the apparent masculine subject عمرانها. The translation assumes the sense of يدنو بها, ‘draws them nearer’; the printed verb may be an error.

On dwellings (diyār), line 2
Such is the world: when it turns its back,it makes its familiar ways unrecognizable.
وهي الدنيا إذا ما أدبرتجعلت معروفها منكرها

معروفها منكرها can contrast the familiar with the unrecognizable, as translated, or suggest kindness turning into ill treatment.

On dwellings (diyār), line 1
The dwellings refuse to speak to you;the rains have altered their traces since I left.
أبت ألا تكلمك الدياروغير رسمها بعدي القطار

The wording أبت ألا تكلمك appears to mean literally ‘refused not to speak to you,’ contrary to the following verse. The translation follows the apparent intended sense; أن تكلمك in place of ألا تكلمك would give that sense.

On dwellings (diyār), line 3
Separation scattered our company, after we had beentogether in the shade of a pleasant life.
فرقت شملنا النوى بعد ما كناجميعا في ظل عيش حميد

Read «كن / اجميعا» across the hemistich break as «كنا جميعًا» ('we were together'); a space is missing before «جميعا».

On dwellings (diyār), line 1
Stop, you two: hold back those mounts, and releasemy tears—after the loss of these homes, shall I conceal my grief?
قفا فاحبسا تلك الركاب وأطلقادموي، فهل بعد الديار أكاتم؟

بعد الديار أكاتم is elliptical and ambiguous. The translation takes بعد as “after,” supplying the loss of the homes and grief as the concealed object. بُعد الديار, “remoteness of the homes,” is another possible reading.

On dwellings (diyār), line 1
O dwellings of my loved ones, for the sorrowful you holdnothing but weeping and greetings of peace.
يا ديار الأحباب ما فيك للمحزون إلا البكاء والتسليم

التسليم can mean offering greetings of peace or submission and resignation; the latter sense is also possible here.

On dwellings (diyār), line 5
You were like the sun of day within those dwellings,shining forth in its zodiacal sign al-Ḥamal.
كنتم كأنكم شمس النهار بهاقد أشرقت وهي من أبراجها الحمل

The syntax of وهي من أبراجها الحمل appears irregular or incomplete. The translation takes it to mean that the sun is in al-Ḥamal (Aries).

On dwellings (diyār), line 7
Time, which gladdened me through them, has indeed grieved me;yet they did no wrong: they grieved me in requital for the joy they gave.
لقد ساءني الدهر الذي سرني بهموما ظلموا ساءوا قصاصا بما سروا

The plural verbs in the second hemistich apparently refer to the departed loved ones, although the first hemistich makes Time the agent. I read ظلموا as active, 'they did wrong'; without vowel marks it could also be passive, 'they were wronged.'

On dwellings (diyār), line 2
Time has left nothing of you but sorrowfor those who remember, and a lesson for whoever looks.
لم يبق منك الدهر إلا حسرةللذاكرين، وعبرة للناظر

The unvocalized عبرة can mean either ‘a lesson’ (ʿibra) or ‘a tear’ (ʿabra); both fit the context.

On dwellings (diyār), line 2
I weep for my family and my homelands, and it grieves methat after them I have neither home nor refuge.
بكيت أهلي وأوطاني وآسفنيأن ليس لي بعدهم دار ولا سكن

Sakan, rendered as “refuge,” can mean a dwelling or someone in whom one finds comfort; either sense is possible here.

On dwellings (diyār), line 1
Dwellings that drank deep of oppression as it was dealt out;death summoned the folk within them and made itself heard.
ديار كرعن الضيم وهو مصرفونادى بهن الموت أهلا فأسمعا

أهلاً is taken as the object of ‘summoned,’ meaning inhabitants. It could instead represent death’s cry of ‘Welcome!’

On dwellings (diyār), line 3
Had the encampment known of those who had scattered,it would have grieved at their loss and lamented.
ولو كان يدري بالذين تفرقواتوجع من فقدانهم وتفجعا

The subject is unstated. The translation takes it to refer to الحي, ‘the encampment,’ in line 2; the antecedent is not certain.

On dwellings (diyār), line 2
How lovely Safwān was as a springtime abode!How often Safwān brought lovers together!
يا حبذا سفوان من متربعولربما جمع الهوى سفوان

«جمع الهوى سفوان» literally says that Safwān ‘gathered love’; ‘brought lovers together’ is an interpretive rendering.

On dwellings (diyār), line 1
Will our former days return, O Laylā,at Dhū al-Rimth—or is there no returning for them?
أراجعة يا ليل أيامنا الألىبذي الرمث، أم لا مالهن رجوع؟

I take يا ليل as a shortened vocative form of Laylā; it could alternatively mean “O night.”

On dwellings (diyār), line 4
Briefly I stayed; then, when the dwellings gave us no answer,I sought consolation for her loss, while tears welled up.
قليلا، فلما استعجمت عن جوابناتعزيت عنها، والدموع ترقرق

قليلا ('briefly') appears to refer back to 'I stood' in line 3. The pronoun in عنها could refer either to the beloved or to the abandoned dwelling-place; the translation takes it as the beloved.

On dwellings (diyār), line 5
I returned to my yearning after forgetting those women,and recognized traces of dwellings that made me weep.
راجعت بعد سلوهن صبابتيوعرفت رسم منازل أبكاني

راجعت is read here as rājaʿtu, ‘I returned to.’ It could instead be rājaʿat, with صبابتي as the subject: ‘My yearning returned after I had forgotten them.’

On dwellings (diyār), line 2
The traces of her dwelling almost smile in recognition—and how many nights and months these dwellings have known!
يكاد من العرفان يضحك رسمهاولكم من ليال للديار ومن شهر

“In recognition” (من العرفان) may suggest the traces recognizing the poet, or their familiarity to him.

On dwellings (diyār), line 2
A dwelling effaced, with no companion in its groundssave remnants of a darkened campsite and tethering-stakes.
دار تعفت، لا أنيس بجوهاإلا بقايا دمنة وأوراي

أوراي appears to be a transposition error for أواري, meaning tethering-places or tethering-stakes; the latter is adopted here.

On dwellings (diyār), line 3
Mayy's abodes! Apart from my companions, there lingeredin my soul troubled thoughts from what they stirred in me.
ديار لمى ظل من دون صحبتيلنفسي مما هيجت لي وساوس

The phrase من دون صحبتي may mean physically apart from his companions, or that these troubled thoughts affected him alone, not his companions.

On dwellings (diyār), line 2
Those are Ṣafrāʾ’s dwellings; there is nofire shining there, nor voices of evening companions.
تلك المنازل من صفراء ليس بهانار تضيء، ولا أصوات سمار

Ṣafrāʾ is treated as the woman’s name here and in lines 5 and 7. It could instead be an epithet referring to her fair complexion.

On dwellings (diyār), line 1
Dwellings deserted by Salmā’s people;may one who cherishes Salmā keep faith with her in love.
ديار أقفرت من آل سلمىرعى سلمى بحسن الوصل راع
