I take رعى سلمى بحسن الوصل راع as a wish or blessing. It could instead be a past-tense statement: someone cherished Salmā with faithful affection. The identity of this راع, literally a keeper or guardian, is unspecified.

On dwellings (diyār), line 2
The winds lingered there every evening,leaving only the remnants of tents, laid in rows,
أربت بها الأرواح كل عشيةفلم يبق إلا آل خيم منضد

آل خيم may refer specifically to surviving tent frames or poles rather than to remnants generally.

On dwellings (diyār), line 1
As for the dwellings, they lingered there but littleonce longing stirred in the pale camels and their riders.
أما الديار فقلما لبثوا بهابعد اشتياق العيس والركبان

“Ishtiyāq al-ʿīs wa-l-rukbān” is grammatically ambiguous: it may mean longing felt by the camels and riders, as translated, or longing for them.

On dwellings (diyār), line 1
Even a brief stay in dwellings where a man is humiliated is nothing but hardship.
وما بعض الإقامة في ديار يهان بها الفتى إلا عناء

بعض الإقامة literally means 'some staying'; it is understood here as a limited duration, hence 'even a brief stay.'

On dwellings (diyār), line 12
O people, how could I surrender control of my affairsover something my heart detests?
فيا للناس كيف ملكت أمريعلى شيء ويكرهه ضميري

ملكت is unvocalized. The translation reads it as mallaktu, ‘I handed over control,’ with the recipient unstated, rather than malaktu, ‘I possessed/controlled.’

On dwellings (diyār), line 4
then many a troop of horsemen have I led on a slender mare,with a mighty steed, stout of limb, keeping abreast of her.
فيا رب خيل قد هديت بشطبةيعارضها عبل الجزارة هيكل

«شطبة» is interpreted as a long, slender mare; the following description is taken to designate another horse keeping alongside her.

On dwellings (diyār), line 2
She came among girls her age, swaying as she walked,with a sandgrouse’s tread, more languid than they and shorter-stepped.
أتت بين أتراب تمايس إن مشتدبيب القطا أوهن منهن أقطف

The compressed phrase «أوهن منهن أقطف» is taken to describe Hind as more languid and shorter-stepped than her companions. The comparison might instead be with the sandgrouse.

On dwellings (diyār), line 2
I swear by the beasts they slaughtered one morning at Minā,beside al-Jimār, weighed down by their hobbles:
إني وما نحروا غداة منيعند الجمار تئودها العقل

I read تئودها as تؤودها, ‘weigh them down,’ taking العقل to mean the sacrificial animals’ hobbles. The supplied spelling appears irregular.

On haunts (maghānī), line 1
Swallow sorrow: the lone sandy tract lies deserted,and let the eye be: longing wrings its tears from it.
تجرع أسى قد أقفر الجرع الفردودع جفه عين يحتلب ماءها الوجد

الجرع الفرد is rendered descriptively as 'the lone sandy tract'; it may instead designate a particular site, al-Jarʿ al-Fard.

On haunts (maghānī), line 2
When the grieving man turns away, his patience worn downby questioning the old dwellings, weeping is his answer.
إذا انصرف المحزون قد فل صبرهسؤال المغاني، فالبكاء له رد

فالبكاء له رد is ambiguous: besides 'weeping is his answer,' it may mean that weeping brings the grieving man back after he turns away.

On haunts (maghānī), line 1
O haunts of youth at Bāb Ḥanāk,not at Raml al-Ghaḍā or Wādī al-Arāk!
يا مغاني الصبي بباب حناكلا برمل الغضا ووادي الأراك

الصبي appears to stand for الصبا, ‘youth,’ which is the reading translated here.

On haunts (maghānī), line 2
It grieves me that Time has decreedyour decay, to my eyes’ distress.
وعزيز علي أن حكم الدهر على رغم ناظري ببلاك

على رغم ناظري literally suggests ‘in defiance of my eye(s).’ The unvocalized ناظري permits either singular or dual.

On haunts (maghānī), line 5
Peace be upon him! I give the ruins no sharein my burning grief or my sobbing.
فعليه السلام لا أشرك الأطلال في لوعتي ولا في نحيبي

The pronoun in عليه is taken to refer to the beloved described in line 4; a reference to the dwelling-place is also possible.

On haunts (maghānī), line 3
For lovers’ custom is to wailin love’s dwelling when the beloved is gone.
فسنة العشاق أن يعولوافي منزل الحب إذا الحب غاب

The unvocalized الحب permits both ḥubb (‘love’) and ḥibb (‘beloved’). The translation reads the first occurrence as ‘love’ and the second as ‘beloved’; both could refer to the beloved.

On haunts (maghānī), line 3
Should Baghdad and its people ask after me,I have ceased to yearn for the people of al-ʿAwāṣim.
متى سألت بغداد عني وأهلهافإني عن أهل العواصم سال

Al-ʿAwāṣim may name the northern Syrian frontier districts or mean 'capital cities' generally. The unvocalized سألت also permits 'you ask Baghdad and its people about me,' rather than making Baghdad and its people the subjects.

On haunts (maghānī), line 2
Yet the Arab youth among themis a stranger in face, hand, and tongue.
ولكن الفتى العربي فيهاغريب الوجه واليد واللسان

The intended sense of 'hand' (Al-yad) is not explicit; it may refer to handwriting. The literal wording is retained.

On haunts (maghānī), line 4
Nothing but blackened stones crouching like sandgrouse,once jet-black, now turned dusty by the wind;
غير حم مثل القطا جاثماتكن جونا فعدن بالريح كدرا

حم denotes black objects, presumably the blackened hearthstones left at the campsite; the noun 'stones' is supplied.

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 3
Since your days, we have found no dwelling like you;may you be watered with bucketfuls of al-Simāk’s rain.
لم نلق مثلك بعد عهدك منزلافسقيت من سبل السماك سجالا

Al-Simāk is a star-name associated here with seasonal rain. The unqualified name can designate Spica (Al-Simāk al-Aʿzal) or Arcturus (Al-Simāk al-Rāmiḥ); the verse does not specify which.

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 3
As though the whole company had never dwelt there, nor been summonedby a resolve to depart, leaving the dwellings bare and empty.
كأن لم يكن فيها الجميع، ولم تصحبهم نية تعري الديار خلاء

I take نية as a resolve to depart, personified as calling the company away. It can also mean an intended destination or direction of travel.

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 2
A tormented man, he paid passion’s debt in tears,distributing them among the dwellings’ faded traces.
معنى قضى دين الغرام مدامعايقسمها في دراسات المنازل

The printed دراسات appears to be a transposition error for دارسات, meaning effaced or faded remains; the translation follows that reading.

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 2
Dwellings—were my bier to pass by them,my spirit would cry, “You two who bear me, pause here with me!”
منازل لو مرت بهن جنازتيلقال الصدى يا حاملي أربعا بيا

Ṣadā, translated as “my spirit,” can mean an echo or the bird associated in old Arab belief with a dead person's spirit. The funeral setting suggests the latter, but “the echo would say” is also possible.

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 1
Do you recognize ruins and a crumbled encircling bank,like an ornate text you trace on parchment?
أتعرف أطلالا ونويا تهدماكخطك في رق كتابا منمنما

Read نويا as نؤيًا: a trench or earthen bank surrounding a tent to keep out rainwater, rendered here as 'encircling bank.'

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 3
Sweeping winds have altered the surface of its soil,and the days have altered what once was clearly marked.
دوارج قد غيرن ظاهر تربهوغيرت الأيام ما كان معلما

دوارج is taken as describing the winds, 'sweeping' or 'passing'; it could instead describe the passing periods of time mentioned in the preceding line.

On ruins (aṭlāl), whole poem

The poet’s lineage is inconsistent in the supplied context: the poet field gives Ṣīnī (صيني), while the introduction gives Ṣayfī (صيفي).

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 1
Whose are these ruins? I did not grieve them, yet they grieved me;they stirred youthful passion—if only they had stirred it in its season!
لمن طلل لم أشجه وشجانيوهاج الصبي، لو هاجه لأوان!

الصبي, here and in line 2, appears to represent الصبا, ‘youthful passion,’ rather than ‘the boy.’ I take the compressed phrase لو هاجه لأوان as a wish: ‘if only they had stirred it at the proper time.’

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 2
Like writing on the forearms of adorned women—the succession of years has changed them,
كالوحي في سواعد الحواليغيرها تناسخ الأحوال

الأحوال can mean either “years” or “conditions”; “years” is adopted here.

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 4
Night showers and morning showers linger,and ill fortune comes round, with good fortune following.
وتلث سارية وغاديةويكر نحس خلفه سعد

نحس and سعد may refer specifically to successive unlucky and lucky stars or periods, rather than to ill and good fortune in general.

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 1
Hind has ruined camps on the rugged ground of al-Sharīf,still visible, though a year has passed since their last occupation.
لهند بحزان الشريف طلولتلوح وأدنى عهدهن محيل

I take محيل to mean ‘a year old’ or ‘having passed through a year’; the reference to the camps’ last occupation is implicit rather than explicit.

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 5
And until I saw the tribe—their open grounds being effacedby a wind from Yaman, laying decay’s warp and weaving it.
وحتى رأيت الحي تعفو عراصهميمانية تسدي البلى وتنير

The opening وحتى (‘and until’) does not connect clearly with the preceding line as transmitted. يمانية is understood as a wind from Yaman. تنير is taken as a weaving term associated with threading the loom, continuing the image introduced by تسدي (‘lays the warp’).

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 2
The south wind and the north have effaced their traces,and a rushing east wind, murmuring its lament.
عفت الجنوب مع الشمال رسومهاوصبا مزمزمة الحنين عجول

عجول is rendered as 'rushing,' but it can also describe a bereaved mother or she-camel. Alongside الحنين ('plaintive yearning'), it may instead personify the wind as grieving.

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 5
May that fellowship never perish! Since they left, time has ageda desolate ruin at Burqat Rāmatayn.
لا يبعدن أنس تقادم بعدهمطلل ببرقة رامتين محيل

The syntax is compressed. I take لا يبعدن أنس as an independent blessing on past fellowship, and طلل in the second hemistich as the delayed subject of تقادم ('has grown old').

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 2
save for enduring hearthstones that never shift, and cold ashes,and a splintered tent peg the young girl drives firmly in with a handstone.
إلى خالدات ما تريم، وهامدوأشعث ترسيه الوليدة بالفهر

The source reads إلى (‘to’), but إلا (‘except for’) appears required by the sense and is followed here.

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 3
I stood there, my eye beset with grit,like an injured eye whose streaming tears never dry.
وقفت بها والعين شاملة القذىكعين طريف ما يجف سجومها

شاملة القذى is an unusual expression, rendered literally as an eye beset with grit. I take طريف to mean someone struck or injured in the eye.

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 4
That stirred my longing for Umm Nawfal,and a host of memories that never leave my soul.
فذلك هاج الشوق من أم نوفلوذكرى لنفس جمة ما تريمها

The syntax of وذكرى لنفس جمة ما تريمها is compressed. I take جمة (‘abundant’) to describe the memories, which do not leave the soul.

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 5
She has indeed gained from me more affection thanshe wished in secret, or her close companion wished.
فقد أدركت عندي من الود فوق ماتمنت بغيب أو تمنى حميمها

بغيب may mean ‘in secret’ or ‘in [my] absence’; the former is used here.

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 1
The traces of Baljāʾ’s folk have faded;separation has grown earnest, and the bond is severed.
عفا من آل بلجاء الطلولوجد البين وانقطع الوسيل

Baljāʾ appears to be a woman’s name; her identity is unknown.

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 4
They watch for departure; when it hastens awaywith the dwellings’ people, and the laden camels move off,
يباصرن النوى فإذا اشمعلتبأهل الدار واقلولى الحمول

The rare verb iqlawlā is rendered 'move off'; its precise force here may be 'rise' or 'hasten away.'

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 3
It is grief enough that I stretched upward to seethe crests of Damkh’s two heights, yet you two cannot be seen.
كفى حزنا أني تطاللت كي أرىذرى علمي دمخ فما تريان

I read تريان as passive تُرَيان, ‘you two are seen,’ taking the phrase as a direct address to the two heights. The unvowelled wording is ambiguous; يُريان, ‘they are seen,’ may instead have been intended.

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 5
Ah, how lovely, by God—if only you two knew it—
ألا حبذا واللهلو تعلمانه

Lines 5–6 appear to be one bayt split incorrectly in the digitized text: ألا حبذا والله لو تعلمانه / ظلالكما يأيها العلمان. The supplied segmentation has been retained.

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 3
It gleams like a young woman’s two hands,the tattoos on her wrists traced afresh.
يلوح كأنه كفا فتاةترجع في معاصمها الوشوم

The unvocalized ترجع is taken here as turajjaʿu, meaning that the tattoos are retraced or renewed; 'return/reappear' is also a possible reading.

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 7
Whenever you say, “His heart will leave Mayya's memory behind,”love for her insists on enduring for all time.
إذا قلت: يسلو ذكر مية قلبهأبى حبها إلا بقاء على الدهر

The unvocalized قلت can mean “I say” or “you say.” The latter is adopted here, retaining the third-person “his heart” in the quoted thought. Mayya is a variant of Mayy in line 1.

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 4
When my eye overflows with tears for it, my companion says:“For a man like you, this is a trial and torment.”
إذا هملت عيني له قال صاحبي:بمثلك هذا فتنة وغرام

The construction بمثلك هذا فتنة وغرام is somewhat ambiguous. The translation takes هذا as referring to the speaker’s longing; غرام can mean consuming passion as well as persistent torment.

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 1
O ruins of Hind, wretched is what you have taken in Hind’s stead!Have you bartered lovely-eyed women for wide-eyed wild cattle and gray ostriches?
أأطلال هند ساء ما اعتضت من هندأقايضت حور العين بالعين والربد

The unvocalized verbs اعتضت and قايضت can be first-person ('I') or second-person ('you'). I read them as addressing the ruins; alternatively, the speaker may be lamenting his own exchange.

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 1
Stop at the effaced ruins, O ʿUlāth;the ropes of those who dwelt there have grown threadbare.
قف بالطلول الدارسات علاثاأضحى حبال قطينهن رثاثا

حبال is translated literally as 'ropes,' presumably tent ropes; figurative 'bonds' with the former inhabitants may also be intended.

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 1
Whose are these buried ruins, their site effaced,their traces vanished save for enduring dark stones?
لمن طلل عافى المحل دفينعفا آيه إلا خوالد جون

عافى appears to represent عافي, meaning effaced or obliterated here. خوالد جون literally means 'enduring dark ones'; I understand this as the blackened hearthstones left at the campsite, though stones are not explicitly named.

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 2
Like doves gathered together at dusk,far from home at nightfall, with no nests.
كما اقترنت عند المساء حمائمغريبات ممسى ما لهن وكون

غريبات ممسى is compressed and somewhat ambiguous: it may describe doves far from home at evening or doves whose evening resting place is unfamiliar.

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 1
ʿAzza’s ruins refuse to speak;her dwelling-places stir the yearning, love-stricken man.
عزة أطلال أبت أن تكلماتهيج مغانيها الطروب المتيما

The opening عزة أطلال appears to lack an initial ل in لعزة أطلال, ‘ʿAzza has ruins.’ The translation assumes this reading.

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 2
How it stirred him—a dwelling where there playedthe trailing skirts of a wild wind racing at dusk!
وما هاجه من منزل لعبت بهلهوجاء مرقال العشي ذيول

The construction وما هاجه من منزل is ambiguous; it is rendered here as an exclamation. The Arabic shifts from addressing 'you' in line 1 to speaking of 'him' here.

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 3
There you once would see Saʿdā, as though she werea fawn just learning to walk, hanging back from the departing herd.
بما قد ترى سعدى به وكأنهاطلا راشح للبارحات خذول

راشح describes a young animal beginning to walk with its mother. للبارحات خذول is less certain: خذول suggests remaining behind or apart from the herd, while البارحات may mean departing animals or, more specifically, game crossing from right to left, traditionally an ill omen.

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 4
I have never seen the like of my eye, withholding its waterfrom me, nor anyone like me, begrudged his tears.
ولم أر مثل العين ضنت بمائهاعلي، ولا مثلي على الدمع يحسد

I read يحسد as passive, “is envied” or “is begrudged,” taking the eye to begrudge the speaker his tears. The unvocalized text also permits an active reading: “envies [others] for their tears.”

On ruins (aṭlāl), line 7
Whoever strives with luck on his side meets good fortune;scant effort does the foolish no harm.
وافق حظا من سعى بجدما ضر أهل النوك ضعف الكد

بجد can mean either 'with good fortune' (bi-jadd) or 'with diligence' (bi-jidd). The following statement about fools prospering despite scant effort favors the former.

On spring camps (rabʿ), line 1
By my life, I spent my nightlike one afflicted with painful illness.
قد لعمري بت ليلىكأخي الداء الوجيع

Read ليلى as ليلي, 'my night'; the final letter appears to be a spelling or digitization error, rather than the name Laylā.

On spring camps (rabʿ), line 2
Grief, my intimate companion,lay nearer to me than my bedmate.
ونجي الهم منيبات أدنى من ضجيعي

The construction نجي الهم is ambiguous: literally 'grief’s confidant,' it is understood here as grief personified as an intimate companion.

On spring camps (rabʿ), line 1
Yes, O dwelling whose people have departed,separation has indeed achieved in you what it sought.
أجل أيها الربع الذي خف آهلهلقد أردكت فيك النوى ما تحاوله

أردكت appears to be a transposition error for أدركت (‘achieved’), the reading translated here.

On spring camps (rabʿ), line 2
The life we wore with its dweller did not remainfresh; even if any life could last, that life would not.
ما دام عيش لبسناه بساكنهلدنا، ولو أن عيشا دام لم يدم

The subject of the final «لم يدم» is implicit. I take it to mean that their former life together would not endure, even if some other life could. «لدناً», literally ‘supple’ or ‘tender’, describes that life as fresh and pleasant.

On spring camps (rabʿ), line 1
Enjoy your ease, house of Barmak,and watch for it—when will it come?
أنعموا آل برمكوارقبوها متى هيه

The wording «وارقبوها متى هيه» is elliptical. The feminine pronoun apparently anticipates the calamity named in line 2; «هيه» is read as «هي» with a pause-ending h.

On spring camps (rabʿ), line 4
Though once you exchanged my misery for comfort,you have now given my eye grit instead of sleep.
وإن كنت قد بدلت بؤسي بنعمةلقد بدلت عيني قذى برقاد

I take the verbs as addressing the dwelling: it formerly relieved the poet's misery but now causes sleepless grief. The unvocalized كنت and بدلت also permit first-person readings; the direction of exchange in the second hemistich is not entirely certain.

On spring camps (rabʿ), line 3
It said: “They all set out and departed,against my will—if only I had had some way to prevent it!”
قال: ساروا بأجمع فاستقلواوبكرهي لو استطعت سبيلا

لو استطعت سبيلا (“if I could find a way”) is elliptical; “to prevent it” supplies the understood wish to prevent their departure.

On spring camps (rabʿ), line 4
As though three doves at the campsitehad alighted, never wearying of their long stay.
كأن حمامات ثلاثا بربعهاوقعن فما يسأمن طول وقوع

The three motionless ‘doves’ may represent the three hearthstones left at the campsite, though the stones are not explicitly named.

On spring camps (rabʿ), line 5
I am indeed lovesick, as you know; yet Iresist some of my soul’s desires.
وإني لصب ما علمت وإننيلبعض هوى نفسي لغير مطيع

The unvocalized ما علمت is taken as ‘as you know’; it could also be read as ‘as far as I know.’

On spring camps (rabʿ), whole poem

The attribution is inconsistent: the poet field names al-Sharīf al-Murtaḍā, while the Arabic introduction names al-Sharīf al-Raḍī.

On spring camps (rabʿ), line 2
And a rough tent peg, split along its back and scarred,worn out, damaged by the serving girl's blows.
وأشعث منقد السراة مهمشاأضر به ضرب الوليدة باليا

The object described is not named; I take it to be an old tent peg, battered by hammering. منقد السراة appears to mean 'split along its back,' and مهمشا 'scratched' or 'scarred.'

On spring camps (rabʿ), line 4
I halted my companions there, myself in sound health; it tookonly a glance before I returned sick.
وقفت به صحبي صحيحا فلم تكنسوى نظرة حتى رجعت بدائيا

I take the unusual بدائيا to represent بِدائي with a final alif lengthening the rhyme: 'with my ailment.'

On spring camps (rabʿ), line 1
My heart's abode lies amid those encampments,as though they had more claim to it than my ribs.
ربع الفؤاد خلال تلك الأربعفكأنها أولى به من أضلعي

The unvocalized opening ربع الفؤاد can also be read verbally: “My heart settled.” I have read ربع as “abode,” which provides an antecedent for “in it” (فيه) in line 2.

On spring camps (rabʿ), line 1
I pass a dwelling where you once lived, as thoughin reverence I were passing the Stone and the Corner.
أمر بربع كنت فيه كأنماأمر من الإجلال بالحجر والركن

The unvocalized كنت can mean either 'I was' or 'you were'; 'you' is adopted here in light of 'your dwelling' in line 2.

On spring camps (rabʿ), line 2
May every cloud pour abundant rain upon you,until you are seen smiling with flowers.
جادتك كل سحابة هطالةحتى ترى عن زهره متبسما

The masculine suffix in زهره ('its flowers') has no clear antecedent: سحابة ('cloud') is feminine, while the dwelling is addressed in the second person. The translation leaves this possessive unresolved.

On spring camps (rabʿ), line 3
Dwellings of Mayy, whose traces have been effaced—you would take their expanses for writing marked with dots.
ديار لمى قد تعفت رسومهاتخال نواحيها كتابا معجما

لمى is read as لِمَيّ, ‘of Mayy.’ معجما is understood as describing writing supplied with distinguishing dots, though an association with foreign or unintelligible writing is also possible.

On spring camps (rabʿ), line 2
I stood there while the riders differed in their views,speaking freely—some excusing me, others reproaching.
وقفت بها والركب شتى سبيلهميفيضون، منهم عاذرون ولوم

I take يفيضون to mean speaking freely, and شتى سبيلهم to describe differing views. The wording could instead describe the riders streaming away along different paths.

On spring camps (rabʿ), line 3
For they were spent before one near who shunned medespite his nearness, and in the wake of one distant, resolved to depart.
فلقد فنين أمام دان هاجرفي قربه، ووراء ناء مزمع

The object of مُزْمِع ('resolved, intent') is unstated; 'resolved to depart' is the likely sense. ناء can mean either 'distant' or 'departing.'

On spring camps (rabʿ), line 3
And say to a heart that has forgotten love: “Return to love,”and to the eye: “Shed your tears, or leave off.”
وقولا لقلب قد سلا راجع الهوىوللعين أذرى من دموعك أودعي

I read أذرى as the feminine imperative أذري, “shed,” addressed to the eye, and أودعي as أو دعي, “or leave off.”

On spring camps (rabʿ), line 4
There is no life like the life we once knew,at a summer abode where we stayed after a spring encampment.
فلا عيش إلا مثل عيش مضى لنامصيفا، أقمنا فيه من بعد مربع

مصيف and مربع can denote summer and spring seasons or the places occupied during them. The translation takes them as seasonal abodes, though a temporal reading is also possible.

On spring camps (rabʿ), line 1
Does the dwelling know what blood it has shed,and what hearts in this caravan it has stirred to longing?
أيدري الربع أي دم أراقاوأي قلوب هذا الركب شاقا

I take the dwelling as the subject of both verbs, and 'this caravan' as qualifying 'hearts.' The unvocalized second hemistich could also mean 'and what hearts this caravan has stirred to longing.'

On spring camps (rabʿ), line 2
The prince of dwellings—you have always been a princessthere over lovely women, in summer and spring.
أمير المغاني لم تزالي أميرةبه للغواني في مصيف ومربع

مصيف ومربع may mean summer and spring quarters rather than the seasons themselves.

On spring camps (rabʿ), line 2
O Lord of the Throne, I have sinned in forsaking her;whatever sin there may be, You are its forgiver.
فذ العرش قد أجرمت في أن هجرتهاوما يك من ذنب فإنك غافره

The feminine pronoun in هجرتها ('forsaking her') has no explicit antecedent; it may refer to an unnamed beloved.

On spring camps (rabʿ), line 1
O dwelling, if only they had been gentle with a man beset by cares,stricken, surrendered to the burning grief of separation!
يا ربع لو ربعوا على ابن هموممستسلم لجوى الفراق سليم؟

ربعوا على can mean either ‘treated gently’ or ‘waited for’; the former is adopted here. سليم, literally ‘sound,’ also denotes someone bitten or stung, and is taken here as ‘stricken’ by love or grief.

On spring camps (rabʿ), line 3
It clothes the site's landmarks in patterned robes it renewsfrom dust; another wind later strips them away.
تكسو معارفه حبرا تجددهمن التراب، وأخرى بعد تستلب

I take أخرى to mean another wind. It could instead imply 'at another time,' with the same wind stripping away what it previously deposited.

On spring camps (rabʿ), line 2
If you now lie deserted, how often you were seeninhabited by them and full of people.
إن تمس وحشا فبما قد ترىوأنت معمور بهم آهل

The compressed phrase فبما قد ترى is understood as contrasting present desolation with former habitation: 'how often you were seen.'

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 5
They were the defenders, and among them weremen of bounty and far-reaching power.
هم كانوا الحماة وكان فيهمذوو الأفضال والأيدي الطوال

الأيدي الطوال, literally “long hands,” may signify great generosity rather than the extensive power adopted here.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 3
Steady the breasts of the sturdy she-camels for a haltamong the standing remnants, as though they were Musnad writing.
أسند صدور اليعملات بوقفةفي الماثلات كأنهن المسند

The unvocalized أسند can be read as an imperative, 'steady,' or as a first-person present, 'I steady.' The imperative is adopted here. المسند is understood as Musnad, the ancient South Arabian script to which the remnants are compared.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 6
Years of union whose long span made one forgetthe thought of parting—as though they were mere days.
أعوام وصل كان ينسى طولهاذكر النوى فكأنها أيام

The unvocalized ينسى is taken as يُنسي, “makes one forget,” with طولها (“their long span”) as its subject.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 5
They have grown accustomed to streaming tears,as though the ruins were the tears’ own lashes.
أنست بإسبال الدموع، كأنها أشفارها

The pronouns in كأنها أشفارها are ambiguous. The translation takes the ruins as resembling eyelashes over which the speaker’s tears flow.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 1
Has the site of a ruined camp stirred you, and dwellingsleft empty, effaced by the scouring rain clouds?
أهاجك مغنى دمنة ومساكنخلت وعفاها المعصرات السوافن

المعصرات السوافن is taken as rain clouds that scour away the traces. المعصرات can also denote rain-bringing winds, and السوافن suggests scraping or sweeping away.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 1
You yearn for Mayy as one yearns for home,called by longing, then forced back by his fetters.
تحن إلى مي كما حن نازعدعاه الهوى فارتد في قيده قسرا

نازع denotes one longing for home; the fetters may suggest a tethered camel, but the referent is not explicit.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 1
O Dārat al-Salam, to whose eastlie old encampment traces whose doves keep making us weep!
يا دارة السلم التي شرقيهادمن يظل حمامها يبكينا

يبكينا is read here as 'makes us weep'; without vowel marks, it could also mean 'weeps for us.'

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 2
I was not the first whose company was scattered,who saw at dawn that parting was certain.
ما كنت أول من تفرق شملهورأى الغداة من الفراق يقينا

The unvocalized كنت could mean 'I was' or 'you were'; the translation adopts the first-person reading.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 3
No indeed! But longing has returned, stirredfor you by ruins whose site has grown old.
ألا لا، ولكن عائد الشوق هاجهعليك طلول قد أحال مقامها

عليك may mean longing stirred 'for you,' addressing the beloved, or longing stirred 'in you.' أحال مقامها may specifically mean that a year has passed over the site, rather than simply that it has grown old.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 2
A remnant of the dwelling of the slayer of handsome youths—nothing is therebut wild beasts, left alone with it, and it with them.
رسم لقاتلة الغرانق ما بهإلا الوحوش خلت له وخلا لها

الغرانق is understood here as handsome young men, whom the beloved figuratively slays; the word can also denote cranes.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 4
Once, O dwelling, you held one who was my solace;since he departed, you have become my solace in his stead.
قد كان يا ربع فيك لي سكنفصرت مذبان بعده سكني

I read مذبان as مذ بان, ‘since he departed.’ سكن can mean a dwelling or someone who provides comfort; سكني in the second hemistich could therefore mean ‘my dwelling’ rather than ‘my solace.’

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 5
I likened the wind-worn tracesof my distant beloved to my own body.
شبهت ما أبلت الرياح من آثارحبيبي النائي إلى بدني

The construction شبهت ... إلى بدني is unusual: شبهت normally takes ب rather than إلى to introduce the object of comparison. I have understood it as ‘I likened ... to my body.’

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 6
I said to my companions: “Was it nearness to themthat the birds foretold, or did their raven cry out parting?”
فقلت لأصحابي: أبا لقرب منهمجرى الطير، أم نادى ببين غرابها!؟

The printed أبا لقرب is read as أبالقرب (“was it nearness…?”), correcting an apparent word-spacing error.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 4
I made the racing of my tears a solace for myself,since I became alone, without companion or dwelling.
صيرت لي من تباري عبرتي سكنامذ صرت فردا بلا إلف ولا سكن

The phrase تباري عبرتي, literally 'the vying of my tear(s),' is unusual; I take it to describe tears racing one another. The unvocalized صيرت could also mean 'you made' rather than 'I made.'

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 2
Ruined camps—cares crowded upon me intheir open grounds, as reproachers crowd.
دمن تكاثرت الهموم على فيعرصاتها، كتكاثر اللوام

على appears to stand for عليّ, ‘upon me,’ which is required by the syntax and is the reading translated here.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 16
From all that I hoped for I have come backsaying: “Bodily health is enough for me.”
وعدت من كل ما أوملهأوقل: حسبي بصحة البدن

أوقل appears to be a transposition error for أقول, “I say.”

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 23
Would that all the life I have lived—since things are as I see them—had never been!
يا ليت ما كان من حياتيإذ ال أمر على ما أراه لم يكن!

إذ ال أمر appears to have faulty spacing or lettering. The translation reads إذ الأمر, “since the situation,” though إذ آل أمر, “since matters have come to,” may also have been intended.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 1
O you two ravens on the dwelling’s traces between us,are you whispering together of parting from ʿAfrāʾ?
ألا يا غرابي دمنة الدار بينناأبا لهجر من عفراء تنتجيان؟

أبا لهجر appears to be a spacing error for أبالهجر, ‘is it of parting …?’

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 3
For ʿAfrāʾ, above all others, has my purest affection,yet ʿAfrāʾ turns away from me and holds back.
فعفراء أصفى الناس عندي مودةوعفراء عني المعرض المتواني

The first hemistich is ambiguous: it may instead describe ʿAfrāʾ as the sincerest of people in her affection, in the speaker’s estimation.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 3
And I remember it—while gray hair flashes its smiling teethamid our locks—the days of youth and reckless daring.
وأذكرها والشيب يضحك ثغرهبلماتنا عهد الشبيبة والفتك

The grammatical connection of «عهد الشبيبة والفتك» ('the days of youth and reckless daring') to «أذكرها» ('I remember it') is compressed and somewhat ambiguous. I take it as specifying the days recalled in connection with the campsite.

On dung-marked traces (diman), line 2
You wept on recognizing its traces,and the raven’s croak stirred longing in you.
بكيت لعرفان آياتهاوهاج لك الشوق نعب الغراب

The unvocalized بكيت could mean 'I wept' or 'you wept'; the latter is adopted to match the following 'in you' (لك).

On traces (rasm), line 2
Effaced: their people have packed upand gone away, while their tent frames remain.
دوارس أما أهلها فتحملوافبانوا، وأما خيمها فمقيم

خيم can denote tents or their wooden frameworks; the latter sense is used here.

On traces (rasm), line 3
When it would accept nothing but weeping in sorrow,I wept until I left not a trace of those remains.
فلما أبى إلا البكاء على الأسىبكيت فما أبقيت للرسم من رسم

The subject of أبى ('would accept nothing') could be either the heart or the speaker's longing.

On traces (rasm), line 3
And three stones in the dwellings, as though they werethree doves perched facing one another.
وغير ثلاث في الديار كأنهاثلاث حمامات تقابلن وقعا

The noun following 'three' is omitted; hearthstones are presumably intended.

On traces (rasm), line 3
There I recalled what had passed; rememberingthe beloved and the traces of home awakens longing.
ذكرت بها ما قدمضى وتذكر الحبيب، ورسم الدار مما يشوق

The printed 'قدمضى' is read as 'قد مضى' ('had passed').

On traces (rasm), line 4
They said, “Parting is only a name;whoever speaks of it means death.”
قالوا: النوى تسميةوالموت يعني من عنى

The syntax of والموت يعني من عنى is compressed and ambiguous. The translation takes الموت as the fronted object: whoever means “parting” really means death.

On traces (rasm), line 1
Long have I lingered by the traces at Tamthūd;they have perished—and all that is new must one day perish.
طال الثواء على رسم بتمثودأودي، وكل جديد مرة مود

طال الثواء literally means “the stay has grown long,” without an explicit personal subject. It may describe the speaker’s lingering at the ruins, as translated, or the long passage of time over them.

On traces (rasm), line 2
The traces have faded, but his heart is not emptiedof an old longing that will not cease and pass away.
عفت الرسوم، وما عفت أحشاؤهمن عهد شوق ما يزول فيذهب

أحشاؤه literally means 'his inward parts,' rendered here as 'his heart.' The third-person pronoun has no explicit antecedent in this excerpt and contrasts with the first person in the surrounding lines.

On traces (rasm), line 5
For some purpose the nights have changed,and for some purpose the stars have turned.
لأمر ما تصرفت اللياليوأمر ما تقلبت النجوم

The second hemistich begins وأمر ما, without the preposition ل found in لأمر ما in the first. The translation assumes parallel meanings; a ل may have been omitted in transmission.

On traces (rasm), line 3
at Jaww, as though you had never dwelt there, nor had there beendesert camps and settlements by the water for your people around it.
بجو كأن لم تحتلله، ولم يكنلأهلك مبدي حوله ومحاضر

I read مبدي as مبدى, a desert camping place, contrasted with محاضر, settlements at watering places.

On traces (rasm), line 2
And fair maidens gathered together, as though they werewild does of al-Malā, wearing fine wraps and saffron-dyed cloth?
وبيض العذارى في جميع، كأنهانعاج الملا يلبس ريطا ومجسدا

يلبس appears grammatically irregular here; the sense suggests يلبسن or تلبس, 'wear,' referring to the maidens or their comparison to wild does.

On traces (rasm), line 2
I questioned them when I was drawn to them, but they would not listenthen to the call of a lover asking for a halt.
وسألتها حين انجذبت فلم تصخفيه لدعوة عاشق مستوقف

The unvocalized مستوقف is taken as active, 'asking for a halt'; it could instead be passive, describing a lover who has been stopped or detained.

On traces (rasm), line 4
I shall surely make tears flow if they shed none,and surely know longing if they do not.
فلأجرين الدمع إن لم تجرهولأعرفن الوجد إن لم تعرف

تجره and تعرف can refer to the ruins or address someone as 'you.' The translation takes the ruins as their subject.

On remains (āthār), line 3
Where is he whose buildings include the two pyramids?Who were his people? When was his final day? Where did he fall?
أين الذي الهرمان من بنيانه؟ما قومه؟ ما يومه؟ ما المصرع؟

“His day” (يومه) is taken here as the day of his death, though it could refer to his time more broadly. “His fall” (المصرع) may refer to the place or manner of his death.

On remains (āthār), line 3
Tell him who forbids what is lawful and permitted: tomorrowyou will, by your honor, be paid in full what you now borrow.
فقل لمن يمنع الحل المباح غداتوفى وحقك ما أصبحت تقترض

I read توفى as تُوَفَّى, 'you will be paid in full.' The debt metaphor is awkward with تقترض, 'you borrow'; the intended sense may instead be that the addressee will have to repay his present debt.

On remains (āthār), line 1
Chickens leap upon her while she kneels,hoping for a gift from Suwayd of Banū Ghubar.
تنزو الدجاج عليها وهي باركةترجو عطاء سويد من بني غبرا

The feminine pronouns apparently refer to the poet’s she-camel, though she is not explicitly named in these verses.

On remains (āthār), line 2
A tribe like a sandal strap, passing along:if they alight on untouched ground, you see no trace.
قبيلة كشراك النعل دارجةإن يهبطوا عفو أرض لا ترى أثرا

دارجة is ambiguous: translated here as 'passing along,' it can also mean 'passing away' or 'dying out.'

On remains (āthār), line 2
Fie on this world of mine! In it I havenever been free of care and torment.
أف لديناي، فإني بهالم أخل من هم وتعذيب

The printed لديناي appears to be a transposition error for لدنياي, “on this world of mine,” which is the reading translated.

On residences, stopping places, haunts, landmarks, waymarks and courtyards, line 3
When they grew grassy and their dwelling-ground flourished,a company of your beloved’s people would be staying there.
وكانت إذ أخلت وأمرع ربعهايكون عليها من صديقك حاضر

أخلت is taken here to mean 'grew grassy,' from الخلى, fresh herbage, rather than 'became empty.' The phrase من صديقك حاضر is also ambiguous: صديقك may mean 'your friend' or 'your beloved,' and حاضر may denote either a settled company or someone present.

On residences, stopping places, haunts, landmarks, waymarks and courtyards, line 2
For I once knew life beneath its shadeLuxuriant, its harvest praised by the scout.
فلقد عهدت العيش في أفيائهافينان يحمد مجتناه الرائد

الرائد ordinarily means a scout seeking pasture and water. Here it appears within the image of life as luxuriant growth yielding a harvest.

On residences, stopping places, haunts, landmarks, waymarks and courtyards, line 6
Whenever I think of union with another, I am held backby yearning for you, and an earlier advocate pleading for you.
وإذا هممت بوصل غيرك ردنيوله عليك وشافع لك أول

The referent of “an earlier advocate” (شافع لك أول) is unspecified; it may mean the speaker’s prior love for her, which argues against a new attachment.

On residences, stopping places, haunts, landmarks, waymarks and courtyards, line 2
As though the east wind fulfills vows when it journeys by night,its trailing skirts visit the place at evening and at dawn.
كأن الصبا توفى نذورا إذا سرتتراوحه أذياله وتباكره

The masculine pronoun in أذياله (‘its trailing skirts’) is unexpected with الصبا (‘the east wind’), normally feminine. The translation takes the skirts to belong to the wind.

On residences, stopping places, haunts, landmarks, waymarks and courtyards, line 7
I have not forgotten the palace’s wild creatures when their herd was startled,when its fawns and wild-cow calves were terrified.
ولم أنس وحش القصر إذ ريع سربهوإذ ذعرت أطلاؤه وجآذره

The palace’s ‘wild creatures,’ ‘fawns,’ and ‘wild-cow calves’ apparently stand metaphorically for its women or young inhabitants; the precise referents are not explicit.

On residences, stopping places, haunts, landmarks, waymarks and courtyards, line 2
If I stay, my mind is journeying;or if I travel freely, my heart is captive.
إما أقمت فإن لبى ظاعنأو سرت منطلقا فقلبي عان

The unvocalized أقمت and سرت could refer either to the speaker ('I stay/travel') or to the addressee ('you stay/travel'); I have taken both as referring to the speaker.

On residences, stopping places, haunts, landmarks, waymarks and courtyards, whole poem

The attribution is inconsistent: the poet field names al-Sharīf al-Raḍī, while the introduction names al-Sharīf al-Murtaḍā.

On residences, stopping places, haunts, landmarks, waymarks and courtyards, line 2
Our sighs and tears suffice youfor rain and breezes after we are gone.
يكفيك من أنفاسنا ودموعناأن تمطري من بعدنا وتراحي

I take the uncommon form «تراحي» to mean being swept by breezes, pairing the lovers’ breaths with wind and their tears with rain.

On residences, stopping places, haunts, landmarks, waymarks and courtyards, whole poem

The feminine pronouns are not explicitly anchored: they may refer to the beloved, her dwelling, or, in the later lines, the “idols of beauty.” The translation uses “her” except where “their” refers directly to those idols.

On residences, stopping places, haunts, landmarks, waymarks and courtyards, line 1
Will you not turn aside for us, that we maysee the deserted grounds or the traces of the tents?
ألستم عائجين لنا لعنانرى العرصات أو اثر الخيام؟

لعنا is understood as a dialectal form of لعلنا, ‘that perhaps we may.’

On the land (arḍ), line 3
If a wind could convey the words of a senderfull of affection, I would confide in the south wind at al-Naqb.
ولو أن ريحا بلغت وحي مرسلحفي لناجيت الجنوب على النقب

I read مرسل حفي as 'a sender full of affection'; the unvocalized مرسل could alternatively mean 'messenger.'

On the land (arḍ), line 1
I see that every land she has dwelt in—even asyears pass over it—has ever more fragrant soil.
أرى كل أرض دمنتها وإن مضتلها حجج يزداد طيبا ترابها

The unvowelled دمنتها permits several readings, including ‘I dwelt in it,’ ‘you dwelt in it,’ and ‘she dwelt in it.’ I have chosen the last in light of the subsequent references to the beloved.

On the land (arḍ), line 1
May God water a land where we clothed ourselves in youththroughout its reaches, and cast off solemnity.
سقى الله أرضا لبسنا الشبابأرجائها وخلعنا الوقارا

The word الشباب appears to be divided across the hemistichs, but a ب is apparently missing at the join. The translation assumes الشباب بأرجائها, “youth throughout its reaches.”

On the land (arḍ), line 5
But for my avoidance of reproach, no drink would be foundto sustain life, nor food, except in my possession.
ولولا اجتناب الذام لم يلف مشربيعاش به إلا لدى ومأكل

لدى is understood as لديّ ('in my possession' or 'with me').

On the land (arḍ), line 2
I find myself yearning, though my people are present,in a beholder’s plain sight and within his hearing.
أراني مشتاقا وأهلي حضرعلى رأي عيني ناظر واستماعه

The syntax of على رأي عيني ناظر واستماعه is unusual. I take عيني ناظر as ‘a beholder’s two eyes’ and the phrase as indicating that the speaker’s people are within sight and hearing.

On the land (arḍ), line 5
Nor did the remoteness of my dwelling deprive me, with him,of his gifts reaching my courtyard and his favor.
وما غلبتني نية الدار عندهعلى رفده في ساحتي واصطناعه

نية الدار is interpreted as the distance or separation of the dwelling. The construction with غلبتني ... على is compressed; I understand it to mean that distance did not prevent the patron’s gifts and favor from reaching the speaker.

On the land (arḍ), line 1
May rain water you, for the sake of something dear to me that dwells in you;were it not for that, I would not grant your soil any rain.
سقيت لمعنى حل فيك أودهولولاه لم أسمح لتربك بالقطر

معنى, literally “meaning” or “something,” appears to be a veiled reference to a beloved person or presence dwelling in the land.

On the land (arḍ), line 2
For you are a land where I have found no contentment,a wretched tract that brings none but the freeborn to ruin.
فإنك أرض ما وجدت بها رضىوحرة سوء ما تضيع سوى الحر

حرة can mean a stony lava tract (Ḥarra) or a freeborn woman (Ḥurra). The wording likely plays on these senses alongside الحر, “the freeborn man”; the translation follows the geographical sense.

On homelands (awṭān), line 2
Rather, I long for homelands far away, and loved onesI have lost; whenever I recall our days together, I yearn.
ولكن أوطانا نأت وأحبةفقدت، متى أذكر عهودهم أصب

The unvocalized أصب is taken as a form of صبا, ‘to yearn’; a passive reading, ‘I am stricken,’ is also possible.

On homelands (awṭān), line 1
Tell al-Ḥārith, rooted in gloryand noble deeds, forefather after forefather,
أبلغ الحارث المردد في المجد وفي المكرمات جدا فجد

المردد appears to describe glory repeatedly inherited through the ancestry. جدا فجد is understood as 'forefather after forefather'; the final word may be missing an alif.

On homelands (awṭān), line 1
I ponder my course, with two resolves: one points east,while the other urges my ambition westward.
أهم ولى عزمان: عزم مشرقوآخر يغري همتي بالمغارب

The unvocalized أهم is taken as 'I ponder [my course]'; it could also convey being troubled or preoccupied.

On homelands (awṭān), line 5
the worst companion.
شر صاحب

This fragment evidently completes the second hemistich of line 4, rather than forming a separate verse. The supplied line division has been retained.

On homelands (awṭān), line 1
O you who dwell far from your homeland,alone, weeping for your home!
يا بعيد الدار من وطنهمفردا يبكي على سكنه

سكن can mean a dwelling or someone in whom one finds comfort, especially a beloved; 'home' is chosen here.

On homelands (awṭān), line 2
Whenever his journey pressed him onward,the ailments in his body grew more severe.
كلما جد النجاء بهجدت الأسقام في بدنه

النجاء denotes swift travel or flight; the verse does not specify whether he is fleeing.

On homelands (awṭān), line 2
So I find solace in the sight of graves, for ingraves like these my brothers and companions of my age have settled.
فأستريح إلى رؤيا القبور، ففيأمثالها حل إخواني وأترابي

رؤيا usually means a dream or vision. Here it is rendered as the sight of graves, but dreaming of graves is also a possible reading.

On homelands (awṭān), line 1
For Āl ʿAbbād it wept—but not as Muḥammad didin his verses—the rain pouring from the clouds.
بكى آل عباد ولا كمحمدبأبياته صوب السحاب إذا همى

The syntax is compressed: I take “the clouds’ downpour” as the delayed subject of “wept,” and “in his verses” as referring to Muḥammad. Muḥammad may be Ibn al-Labbāna himself, whose given name was Muḥammad, or the poet-king al-Muʿtamid Muḥammad ibn ʿAbbād. بأبياته could alternatively mean “at his dwellings,” yielding a different construction.

On homelands (awṭān), line 9
I remain steadfast in my wont; and if I die,I shall leave my traces as a gathering-place for mourners.
وإني على رسمي مقيم، فإن أمتسأترك للباكين رسمي موسما

رسم can mean an established practice or a remaining trace. The line appears to shift between these senses; the final “traces” may specifically suggest the poet’s grave. موسما is understood as a place where mourners gather or return.

On homelands (awṭān), line 2
and grants me my dwelling places,and sets me in my homelands,
وأعطاني أعطانيوأوطاني أوطاني

The repeated forms appear to be wordplay: أعطاني أعطاني, ‘grants me my dwelling places,’ with the second word understood as أعطانِي (literally, my camels’ resting places beside water). أوطاني أوطاني apparently means ‘sets me in my homelands’; the first form may represent أوطأني with the hamza omitted.

On homelands (awṭān), line 2
Then raise your voices; on the fifth morning let us see,at Qarqarā, what anguish the soul feels for its homeland.
ثم ارفعا الصوت ننظر صبح خامسةبقرقري، ما عناء النفس بالوطن

«ما عناء النفس بالوطن» is ambiguous: it may express anguish over the homeland, as translated, or ask rhetorically what hardship the soul could feel when at home.

On homelands (awṭān), line 5
O tamarisks of the plain, my companions have grown wearyof my staying; is there a place for a midday rest in your shade?
ويا أثلات القاع قدمل صحبتيمقامي، فهل في ظلكن مقيل

The printed «قدمل» is read as «قد ملّ». «صحبتي» is understood as “my companions,” the subject, and «مقامي» as “my staying,” the object.

On homelands (awṭān), line 7
I wish to return to you, but I am held back,whenever I attempt it, by a heavy debt upon me.
أريد رجوعا نحوكم فيصدنيإذا رمته دين على ثقيل

The printed «على» is read as «عليّ» (“upon me”), modifying the debt.

On homelands (awṭān), line 2
Whenever my eye glimpses the lightning of al-Shām, andthe skirts of darkness are drawn back from it in the distance,
وإن شام برق الشام طرفي وشمرتعلى البعد عنه للظلام ذيول

I read شمرت as passive, 'were drawn back.' The placement and relation of على البعد عنه are compressed; I understand the distant lightning as parting the darkness.

On homelands (awṭān), line 3
My heart is checked before it flies away with longingby fingers slender as the shaft of a reed.
تدارك قلبي أن يطير صبابةبنان كأنبوب اليراع نحيل

I take بنان, 'fingers,' as the subject of تدارك, checking the heart before it flies away. Whose fingers these are is not explicitly stated.

On homelands (awṭān), line 3
I wander as a speck of dust wanders in an eye,and journey by night, while the night-roaming star is bewildered on the horizon.
أجول، كما جالت قذاة بمقلةوأسرى، وسارى النجم في الأفق حيران

I read أسرى and سارى as أسري (“I journey by night”) and ساري (“night-roaming”), respectively, understanding ساري النجم as a star traveling through the night sky.

On homelands (awṭān), line 8
I lived among them for a time under the affiliation I claimed,my honor intact, my sleep more than fitful dozing.
جاورتهم زمنا فيما دعوت بهعرضي صحيح ونومي غير تهجاع

The phrase فيما دعوت به is compressed and ambiguous. I take it to refer to the tribal affiliation the speaker claimed, in keeping with the introductory account of his assumed identities.

On homelands (awṭān), line 1
I lodged, praise be to God, among the finest clan;I rejoice in their goodness and modesty.
نزلت بحمد الله في خير أسرةأسر بما فيهم من الخير والخفر

الخفر is read as khafar, “modesty.” Without vowel marks it could also be khafr, “protection,” which would suit the context of taking refuge.

On homelands (awṭān), line 5
Or of the tribe of Qaḥṭān?” Such questioning is folly;so Rawḥ and his companion Zufar said to me.
أو الحي قحطان، فتلكم سفاهةكما قال لي روح وصاحبه زفر

“So Rawḥ and his companion Zufar said” is taken to refer back to the questions about tribal ancestry, rather than to the judgment that such questioning is folly.

On homelands (awṭān), line 5
When deliverance is decreed for a young man,the wound heals, and hurt is a small thing.
وإذا الفتى كتب النجاء لهفالكلم يعفو والأذى جلل

النجاء can mean deliverance or swift travel; I have understood it as deliverance here.

On homelands (awṭān), line 2
one who turns a distracted gaze toward his homeland,now yielding to its pull, now resisting;
يكر إلى الأوطان طرفا موزعايلين لها طورا وطورا يمانع

I take the third-person verbs in lines 2–3 as continuing the description of the wavering man whom the speaker denies resembling, rather than describing the speaker himself.

On homelands (awṭān), line 1
How wondrous the phantom that visited a band of youths,their heads bent over the camel-saddles!
لله ما طيف ألم بفتيةتحنو رؤوسهم على الأكوار

The wording لله ما طيف is unusual; it is taken here as an exclamation of wonder at the visiting phantom.

On homelands (awṭān), line 3
Homelands do not turn him from his purpose, nordoes longing guide him to the dwelling’s traces.
لا تلفت الأوطان عزمته ولايهدي الحنين إلى رسوم الدار

يهدي الحنين is taken as ‘longing guides [him],’ with the object understood. It could alternatively be read يُهدي الحنينَ, ‘he offers his longing,’ yielding ‘nor does he offer his longing to the dwelling’s traces.’

On homelands (awṭān), line 4
then everything but piety ill becomes him,and whatever else he persists in is ugliest of all.
فكل شيء سوى التقوى به سمجوما أقام عليه فهو أسمجه

The final hemistich is compressed and ambiguous, particularly the pronoun in أسمجه. I take ما أقام عليه to mean whatever conduct other than piety he persists in, with persistence making it especially unseemly.

On homelands (awṭān), line 4
They speak of no one's shortcomings in my presence,nor, when my hands give generously, do they restrain me.
لا يحضران امرءا عندي بمنقصةولا إذا جادت الكفان كفاني

لا يحضران امرءا عندي بمنقصة literally suggests bringing someone before the speaker with a fault attributed to him. I take it to mean that the companions do not disparage others in his presence.

On homelands (awṭān), line 10
How many an envious man has been consumed by what he sees ofmy merit; how many a hater has choked with grief at my fortunes!
كم قد وري من حسود ما يعاين منفضلي، وكم قد شجى من شأني شاني

وري appears to be وَرِيَ, referring to an internal consuming disease or ulceration, here caused figuratively by envy. “Has been consumed” reflects this reading.

On cities (mudun), line 3
They departed before us, and we follow in their tracks.
سبقونا إلى الرحي_ل، وإنا لبالأثر

الرحي_ل contains an intrusive underscore and has been read as الرحيل, ‘departure.’

On cities (mudun), line 3
It was as though destruction had settled in its courtyard,or Time had assailed it with an angry man’s onslaught.
فكأنما سكن الفناء فناءهاأوصال فيها الدهر صولة مغضب

Read «أوصال» as «أو صال» (“or [Time] assailed”); the words appear to have been joined through a spacing error.

On cities (mudun), line 2
Had they answered you, they would have said—knowing the ways of those who have passed away and those who remain—
فلو أجابتك قالتوهي عالمة بسيرة الذاهب الماضي ومن غبرا

غبر can mean either ‘remained’ or ‘passed away.’ ‘Those who remain’ is adopted here, but ‘those who passed away’ is also possible.

On cities (mudun), line 4
when they defended my honor wheneverdarkness fell upon a band of men craving milk.
إذ هن عن حسبي مذاود كلمانزل الظلام بعصبة أعيام

أعيام is understood as describing men craving milk, from the root عيم. The implied defense of the speaker’s honor appears to be the camels’ provision of milk for guests.

On cities (mudun), line 6
and dwell beside those men with whose arrowsI shoot the enemy when an archer wrongs me:
وتجاوري النفر الذين بنبلهمأرمى العدو إذا تهضم رام

The wording إذا تهضم رام is ambiguous. The translation takes رام as “an archer” and تهضم as “acts unjustly toward”; the object “me” is inferred.

On cities (mudun), line 7
those who freely give,when you ask, their inherited wealth,
الباذلينإذا طلبت تلادهم

The supplied lines 7–8 appear to divide one bayt irregularly: الباذلين إذا طلبت تلادهم / والمانعي ظهري من العرام. The supplied divisions have been preserved.

On countries (bilād), line 2
A land where I wore out the mount of youth,and its days and months were gentle with us.
بلاد بها أنضيت راحلة الصبيولانت لنا أيامها وشهورها

الصبي is read as الصِّبا, 'youth,' in the metaphor 'the mount of youth.' The printed spelling may be an error; read literally, it could mean 'the boy.'

On countries (bilād), line 1
And an exile whose night passesin varied woes, while his eye sheds tears.
ومغترب ينقضي ليلهفنونا ومقلته تدمع

فنونا literally means 'in various kinds or forms'; what varies is unstated. 'In varied woes' takes it as referring to changing forms of distress.

On countries (bilād), line 2
A land where those I love dwell; yet Iturn with fate wherever it turns.
بلاد بها أهل الهوى غير أننيأميل مع الأقدار حيث تميل

أهل الهوى could mean 'lovers' generally rather than 'those I love.'

On countries (bilād), line 3
Never have I seen such companionship turn, after him, to desolation,or such coolness upon the heart turn to burning thirst.
ولم أر أنسا بعده صار وحشةوبردا على الأكباد صار غليلا

The negative construction ولم أر is awkward in context. I have understood it as an expression of astonishment, supplying an implied comparison ('such'); read strictly literally, it would deny having seen companionship turn to desolation.

On countries (bilād), line 1
Doom drove you to Dimashq, thoughDimashq had never been a homeland for our people.
الحين ساق إلى دمشق وماكانت دمشق لأهلنا بلدا

The object of ساق ('drove') is unstated; 'you' is inferred from the second-person address in line 2.

On countries (bilād), line 4
Life, for one whose loved ones have departed,offers no contentment, nor is he counted among the living.
وما الحياة لمن بانت أحبتهرضي، ولا هو في الأحياء معدود

رضي is read as رِضًى (‘contentment’); the printed spelling appears irregular here.

On countries (bilād), line 1
If God waters any land with a morning cloud’s downpour,may He water those lands with nothing but blazing fire.
إذا سقى الله أرضا صوب غاديةفلا سقاهن إلا النار تضطرم

The feminine plural pronoun in سقاهن, rendered 'those lands,' has no explicit antecedent in this excerpt.

On countries (bilād), line 8
Since leaving them, I have met and tested no tribethat did not make me love them all the more.
لم ألق بعدهم حيا فأخبرهمإلا يزيدهم حبا إلى هم

The ending إلى هم is grammatically awkward as printed. The translation reads إلى as إليّ, 'to me,' and takes the general sense to be that acquaintance with other tribes increases the speaker’s affection for his former companions.

On countries (bilād), line 1
Leave their lands, for there they have grown weary—my pale camels—of the barrenness of my night-halt and camping place.
سر عن بلادهم فقد سئمت بهاعيسى محول معرسي ومناخي

The printed عيسى appears to represent عِيسي, 'my pale camels,' rather than the name ʿĪsā. I take محول as مُحول, 'barrenness' or 'drought.'

On countries (bilād), line 2
Abandon hopes: they are deceitful,and their promises are snares for those who yearn.
ودع الأماني إنها غرارةووعودها للراغبين أواخ

I take أواخ as أواخٍ, a plural of آخية/أخية, a tether or tethering loop, used figuratively here for snares.

On countries (bilād), line 3
Is there any glory in my leaving lands that have turned hostile—for one like me, or for those who dwell there?
وهل في ارتحالي عن بلاد تنكرتلمثلي أو للساكنين بها فخر؟

The attachment of لمثلي is ambiguous. I take it with فخر, parallel to للساكنين بها: 'glory for one like me, or for those who dwell there.' It could instead qualify تنكرت: 'lands that turned hostile to one like me,' though this leaves the coordination with أو less straightforward.

On countries (bilād), line 3
Then she said to maidenslike the gazelles of al-Rahīn:
م قالت لفتيات كآرام الرهين:

The initial م appears incomplete; ‘Then’ assumes an intended ثم.

On countries (bilād), line 3
Keep delight alive with wineand drinking it as long as you live.
واحى اللذاذة بالمدام وشربها مادمت حيا

I read واحى as وأَحْيِ, meaning 'keep alive' or 'revive'; the printed spelling appears irregular.

On countries (bilād), line 4
Whatever intimate or companion reproached me for this love,that companion or intimate was sent away without hope.
ومن لامني فيه حميم وصاحبفرد بيأس صاحب وحميم

The syntax is compressed and فرد is unvocalized. I read it as passive fa-rudda, 'was sent away,' with the reproaching friend left without hope of changing the speaker's devotion.

On countries (bilād), line 3
for your sake my soul finds solace in solitary places,as one alone finds solace in company.
إلى الخلوات تأنس فيك نفسيكما أنس الوحيد إلى الجميع

فيك is ambiguous here: 'for your sake,' 'because of you,' or 'through you' are possible readings.

On countries (bilād), line 1
There is no lover secure in his beloved,nor anyone in love, whom time will not bereave.
وما من حبيب آمن لحبيبهولا ذي هوى إلا له الدهر فاجع

آمن لحبيبه may mean trusting his beloved or feeling secure concerning the beloved; the translation follows the latter reading.

On countries (bilād), line 5
I pass my day in conversation and wishes,and night brings me together with sorrow—night is a gatherer.
أقضي نهاري بالحديث وبالمنىويجمعني والهم والليل جامع

The syntax of ويجمعني والهم والليل جامع is compressed. I understand night as the agent that brings the speaker and sorrow together.

On the house (dār), line 3
No one trusts this world and its daysafter me, except an ignorant fool.
ما يأمن الدنيا وأيامهابعدي إلا أنوك جاهل

“After me” translates بعدي literally. The speaker may be the ruined dwelling itself, meaning “after seeing what has happened to me,” but this is not explicit.

On the house (dār), line 3
Such is this abode: hopes are nothing but sorrowson its account, and pleasures nothing but calamities.
هي الدار ما الآمال إلا فجائععليها وما اللذات إلا مصائب

The attachment of عليها is somewhat ambiguous. Here it is taken with فجائع: sorrows suffered on account of this worldly abode.

On the house (dār), line 2
Though you are bereft of my revelry and my dwelling there,you have become peopled by my anguish and sorrows.
لئن تعطلت من لهوي ومن سكنيلقد تأهلت من بثي وأشجاني

سكني is ambiguous without vowel marks: it can mean 'my dwelling/residence,' as translated here, or 'my beloved,' someone in whom the speaker finds comfort.

On the house (dār), line 1
You have indulged too much in life and hopes for it,yet death has cruel ways.
أفرطت في العيش وتأميلهوللمنايا شيم نكد

The unvocalized أفرطت permits either 'I have indulged too much' or 'you have indulged too much'; the second-person reading is adopted in light of the letter's address.

On the house (dār), line 2
A man's life is only a moment,with none of it before that moment or after.
وإنما عيش الفتى ساعةلا قبلها منها ولا بعد

The compressed wording لا قبلها منها ولا بعد is grammatically ambiguous; it is taken here to mean that life consists only of the present moment.

On the house (dār), line 2
The abode only heightened your yearning;youth is not the same as feigning youth.
لم تزدك الدار إلا طرباوالصبي غير شبيه بالتصابي

الصبي normally means “the boy.” The contrast with التصابي (“acting young”) suggests that الصبا or الصبى (“youth”) is intended, and the translation follows that reading.

On the house (dār), line 2
A darkened trace in the dwelling has struck my eye,visited in turn by the seasons with wind and rain.
لقد طرفت في الدار عيني دمنةتعاورها الأزمان بالريح والقطر

Ṭarafat … ʿaynī literally suggests striking or pricking the eye. The ruined trace may be described as painfully affecting the poet's sight, rather than merely catching his eye.

On the house (dār), line 2
No trace remains, save what you recall or see:withered thumām grass around the places where the tents stood.
فلا عهد إلا أن تذكر أو ترىثماما حوالي نصب الخيم باليا

نصب الخيم is ambiguous: it may refer to the pitching sites of the tents or to their upright supports. The translation follows the former reading.

On the house (dār), line 3
May spring brighten your valley, for oftenwe dwelt there and saw it as the loveliest of valleys.
وأنار واديك الربيع، فربمانغني به ونراه أبهج واد

نغني is understood as نغنى, 'we dwelt,' rather than 'we sing,' in keeping with the context.

On the house (dār), line 1
Does he question the dwelling’s traces, when the dwelling is his heart?How could it contain the longing his heart holds?
أيسأل رسم الدار، والدار قلبهوأنى لها ما قد حواه من الوجد؟

The pronoun references are somewhat ambiguous. I take لها to refer to the dwelling and the subject of حواه to be his heart.

On the house (dār), line 3
The enjoyment of loved ones is only a passing solace:it gathers only to scatter, and brings near from afar.
وما متعة الأحباب إلا تعلةتلم لتشتيت وتقرب عن بعد

The unvocalized تلم can mean either “gathers together” or “visits briefly”; I have chosen the former. عن بعد may mean “from afar” or “after separation.”

On the house (dār), line 2
Would that cure a heartache that has set my innards aflamewith its burning, and drawn abundant tears with its restless stirrings?
أفي ذاك برء من جوى ألهب الحشىتوقده، واستغزر الدمع جائله

The expression جائله is compressed and somewhat ambiguous. It is taken here as the heartache’s restless movement or stirring, which draws abundant tears.

On the house (dār), line 1
Night and day passed over Fahmibn ʿAmr, till they became like a field cut bare.
درج الليل والنهار على فهم بن عمرو فأصبحوا كالصريم

Al-ṣarīm is ambiguous: it can mean a harvested or devastated field, but also the darkness of night. The translation adopts the image of a field stripped bare.

On the house (dār), line 1
O dwelling, what have the days done to you?They have left no cheer in you worth seeking.
يا دار ما فعلت بك الأياملم تبق فيك بشاشة تستام

تستام is understood as 'sought after,' though it may retain the commercial sense of being valued or priced.

On the house (dār), line 5
I attained all that a man can attain in his youth;yet the bloom of all that proved to be sin.
وبلغت ما بلغ امرؤ بشبابهفإذا غضارة كل ذاك أثام

أثام is translated as 'sin'; it can also mean the penalty or requital for sin.

On the house (dār), line 2
Horse-tethering stakes, now effaced, and campsiteswhere a noble clan rested at evening, then went far away.
أواري خيل قد عفت ومنازلأراح بها حي كرام وأعزبوا

أراح بها and أعزبوا may refer specifically to livestock: bringing the herds back there at evening and subsequently driving them to distant pasture, rather than simply resting and departing.

On the house (dār), line 9
My lingering had grown long as I held back a tearover a ruined campsite where my soul had nearly fled.
وقد طال توقا في أكفكف عبرةعلى دمنة كادت بها النفس تزهق

توقا في appears to be a mistaken division of توقافي, understood as “my lingering” or “my prolonged standing.”

On the house (dār), line 2
Within you, the east wind has departed from its natureand its gentleness: its breeze is now a gale.
وتغيرت فيك الصباعن خلقهاوليانها، فنسيمها إعصاف

The source’s الصباعن appears to omit a space; read as الصبا عن, “the east wind … from.”

On the house (dār), line 1
Death has folded away what bound me to Muḥammad,and none can unfold what death folds away.
طوى الموت ما بيني وبين محمدوليس لما تطوى المنية ناشر

Muḥammad's identity is not established by the excerpt.

On the house (dār), line 1
How long shall I keep halting and journeying,and fretting over a livelihood, through its ebb and flow?
إلى متى أنا في حل وترحالوهم عيش بإدبار وإقبال

بإدبار وإقبال may refer to the ebb and flow of his livelihood, as translated, or to his own coming and going.

On the house (dār), line 1
A youth whose brow was like the full moon in the dark of night—over him rose mourners and dust-bearing winds.
وفتى كأن جبينه بدر الدجىقامت عليه نوائح وروامس

روامس is understood here as winds that cover or efface traces with dust; it could also mean those who bury or cover the dead.

On the house (dār), line 2
He planted palm-shoots, hoping for a long life;the palm-shoots lived, but the horseman died and left them.
غرس الفسيل مؤملا لبقائهفحيا الفسيل ومات عنه الفارس

لبقائه is taken to refer to the planter's hoped-for survival, though the pronoun could instead refer to the survival of the palm-shoots.

On the house (dār), line 2
He lived in an abode, though his true home lay elsewhere;it beguiled him with hopes, then he departed.
كان في دار سواها دارهعللته بالمنى، ثم انتقل

The compressed phrase «سواها داره» is read here as “his home was elsewhere,” apparently contrasting his earthly dwelling with the grave.

On the house (dār), line 4
Truly, it is a beloved whose affection does not last,while its lover never ceases to yearn.
لمعشوقة ودها لا يدوم، وعاشقها أبدا غير سال

I take the initial lām in لمعشوقة as emphatic. It could instead mean 'for a beloved,' linking this line to 'our striving' in the preceding line.

On the house (dār), line 1
Question the dwelling, if you would question one who knows;seek refuge in tears, and you will call upon a protector.
سائل الدار إن سألت خبيراواستجر بالدموع تدع مجيرا

بالدموع may mean seeking refuge in tears themselves or using tears to appeal for protection.

On the house (dār), line 4
They gazed toward the tribe that stayed behind, with eyesdrinking their fill of flowing tears.
ورنوا إلى الحي المقيم بأعينينهلن من ماء الدموع الجاري

ينهلن can suggest drinking one's fill or, when said of eyes, shedding tears. I have retained the drinking image suggested by من ماء الدموع, 'from the water of tears.'

On the house (dār), line 1
O bewilderment of the soul! Which way have they gone—those who dwell in the depths of my heart?
يا حيرة النفس أنى وجهة سلكواومن هم في سواد القلب حلال

The wording ومن هم at the start of the second hemistich is syntactically awkward. I take it as referring back to those who departed: 'those who dwell in the depths of my heart.'

On the house (dār), line 2
May the sweetness of nights gone by return there,and the bliss of a life whose lush abundance has passed away.
وعاد بها طيب الليالي التي خلتوغبطة عيش قد تقضت غياطله

The rare word غياطله appears to evoke luxuriant or tangled growth; its figurative sense here is rendered as 'lush abundance.'

On the house (dār), line 8
And a herd of gazelles, with the sun kept from them,their noble does screened even from an apparition in a dream.
وسرب ظباء تحجب الشمس دونهوتحجب عن طيف الخيال عقائله

تحجب الشمس دونه is somewhat ambiguous. I take it to mean that the sun is kept from reaching the gazelles, rather than that their beauty eclipses it.

On the house (dār), line 9
And every noble man of valor whom you would think—whenever he drew his blade—a sword burnished by its polishers.
وكل أخي بأس كريم تخالهإذا ما انتضى سيفا جلته صياقله

I take سيفاً as the delayed complement of تخاله ('you would think him a sword'), with إذا ما انتضى parenthetical ('whenever he drew his blade'). The unvocalized syntax also permits taking سيفاً as the object of انتضى, but that leaves the comparison less explicit.

On the house (dār), line 1
They say, “You have wailed enough over the dwelling;there is no help in lamenting an effaced encampment.
يقولون: قد أعولت في الدار ما كفاوليس على ربع عفا بمعول

معول can denote lamentation or something relied upon. The translation takes the phrase to mean that lamenting an effaced encampment offers no help.

On the house (dār), line 5
a dream.
حلم

حلم ('a dream') evidently completes the sentence and verse in line 4, rather than forming a separate verse. The supplied division is preserved.

On the house (dār), line 1
Indeed, a man whose home is now in Irbil,while his brothers and his heart’s attachments are in Shayzar,
وإن امرأ أضحت بإربل دارهوفي سيزر إخوانه وشجونه

شجونه can mean his cares, sorrows, or attachments; “his heart’s attachments” follows the last sense here.

On the house (dār), line 3
After their departure, there remainedthe limbs of a lovelorn one, the rest of him gone.
وتخلفت من بعد فرقتهمأوصال صب سار سائره

سار سائره is ambiguous: literally, either 'the rest of him departed' or 'his traveling part departed.' It appears to contrast the lover's remaining body with his heart or inward self, which has gone with the departing companions.

On the house (dār), line 2
Dull-colored, windblown, rain-drenched—From the days when a wide-eyed woman was the joyful man's delight.
مكتئب اللون مراح ممطورأزمان عيناء سرور المسرور

عيناء is translated as the epithet 'wide-eyed woman'; it could instead be the woman's name, ʿAynāʾ.

On the house (dār), line 3
Wide-eyed and dark-eyed, among wide-eyed, dark-eyed women. [Another said:]
عيناء حوراء من العين الحور وقال آخر

وقال آخر ('Another said:') appears to be an editorial introduction to the next quotation, accidentally included in the verse. It is translated in brackets.

On the house (dār), line 4
And a slender youth, after long exhaustion,is swayed by the fatigue of night travel, as though drunk.
وأغيد من طول الكلال يميلهكلال السرى حتى كأن به سكرا

أغيد describes someone or something supple and gracefully bending. A slender youth is assumed here, but the referent is not explicit; a mount may be intended instead.

On the house (dār), line 1
He offered tears to an abode and was true to it;for dwellings have a share of the tears that flow.
أهدى الدموع إلى دار وماصحهافللمنازل سهم من سوافحها

أهدى is translated as a past-tense verb, 'he offered.' It may instead represent أهدي, 'I offer,' which would agree with the first-person voice in line 2.

On the house (dār), line 2
You stayed there, doubled over a liverseared through, a hand resting upon its covering.
ظلت بها تنطوي على كبدنضيجة فوق خلبها يدها

I read ظلت as the contracted second-person masculine ظَلْتَ, ‘you stayed.’ The possessive in يدها (‘its/her hand’) is awkward: its apparent antecedent is the liver, although the hand presumably belongs to the lover. خلب denotes the membrane covering the liver.

On the house (dār), line 2
Though you have become a field for sand-laden winds,I have become a field for cares.
لئن أصبحت ميدان السوافيلقد أصبحت ميدان الهموم

The unvocalized أصبحت permits either “you have become” or “I have become.” I read the first as addressing the abode and the second as referring to the speaker; the second could also continue addressing the abode.

On the house (dār), line 4
They say, “We shall grow rich”; yet, by God, wealthis only what keeps one from begging and supplies one’s needs.
يقولون: نستغني، ووالله مال الغنىمن المال إلا ما يعف وما يكفي

مال الغنى appears to contain an extra ل; the translation assumes ما الغنى, “wealth is nothing but…”.

On the house (dār), line 3
And whether my brimming eye overflowedfor your sake, until its tears drenched my cloak.
وهل فاضت العين الشروق بمائهامن أجلك حتى اخضل من دمعها بردى؟

I read بردى as بُردي, “my cloak,” with final ى standing for ي.

On the house (dār), line 9
Though the days bring changes between us, Mayy,I shall neither forget our pledge nor change.
فإن تحدث الأيام يا مي بيننافلا ناسيا عهدا ولا متغير

ناسيا and متغير have apparently mismatched case forms. The translation assumes an implicit first-person construction: 'I shall neither forget ... nor change.'

On the house (dār), line 1
Ask the luxuriant bān-tree on the sandy ground wherethe bān-trees grow: did I greet the ruins of your dwelling?
سلى البانة الغناء بالأجرع الذيبه البان، هل حييت أطلال دارك؟

The unvocalized حييت, like قمت and اخترت in line 2, permits either a first-person or a second-person reading. I take the speaker to be asking his beloved to question the tree about his own actions.

On the house (dār), line 6
I realized that no dwelling after ʿĀlijcould bring joy, and no beloved after Zaynab.
تبينت أن لا دار من بعد عالجتسر، وأن لا خلة بعد زينب

«خلة» is read as “beloved,” though the unvocalized word could also mean intimate friendship or affection.

On the house (dār), line 2
May your new attachment at Ḥuzwā bring you no joy,distracting you from the desolate traces at Rāmatayn.
لا هناك الشغل الجديد بحزوىعن رسوم برامتين قفار

I read «لا هناك» as «لا هنأك», with the hamza unrepresented: 'may it bring you no joy.'

On the house (dār), line 1
Is it right, if al-Rabāb’s home has grown distant,or a bond has snapped, that your heart should take flight?
أألحق إن دار الرباب تباعدتأو انبت حبل أن لبك طائر

The opening أألحق appears irregularly written. I understand it as an interrogative construction, 'Is it true/right …?', with إن introducing the condition and أن introducing 'your heart should take flight.'

On the house (dār), line 7
Then blame yourself: you did what you did willingly,and made common cause with error while wandering heedlessly.
فنفسك، لم جئت الذي جئت طائعاوحالفت أمر الغي إذ أنت سادر؟

I read لم as لُمْ, 'blame,' rather than لِمَ, 'why.' This fits both the syntax and the meter, despite the supplied final question mark.

On the house (dār), line 2
I did not choose to dwell far from you because my love had faded;rather, the decrees of fate have tangled courses.
وما اخترت نأي الدار عنكم لسلوةولكن مقادير لهن شجون

شجون can mean branching or tangled paths, but also sorrows; the latter sense may also be intended here.

On the house (dār), line 5
Go off with it—go off with it!It is hung about your neck like a dove’s collar.
اذهب بها أذهب بهاطوقتها طوق الحمامة

أذهب is treated as a repetition of the preceding imperative اذهب despite the different hamza spelling. طوقتها is read passively: ‘you have been collared with it.’

On the house (dār), line 2
Bakr ibn Wāʾil lodged you in the midst of their dwellingand extended kindness to you when you were in the wrong.
لقد وسطتك الدار بكر بن وائلوضمت لك الإحسان إذ أنت مجرم

The unusual construction وسطتك الدار is understood as ‘lodged you in the midst of their dwelling,’ with Bakr ibn Wāʾil as the subject.

On the house (dār), line 4
Whenever it visits a dwelling of Zaynab, it returnsthere to longing, until its buried sorrow is revealed.
إذا غشيت ربعا لزينب راجعتبه الشوق، حتى يستبان دفينها

The unvocalized غشيت and راجعت can address 'you' or refer to the feminine noun 'soul' in line 3. I have taken the soul as their subject. 'Sorrow' is supplied for the unspecified thing buried within it (دفينها).

On the house (dār), line 3
Will you forever keep dying of grief for Laylā,at a stopping place where you stood, or beside a dwelling?
ما تبرح الدهر من ليلى تموت جفافي موقف وقفته أو على دار؟

The unvocalized وقفته can mean either 'where you stood' or 'where she stood'; the translation adopts the former.

On the house (dār), line 2
We questioned its dwelling-grounds, and turned awaywith an ailment, though we had consulted no physician.
وسألنا ربوعها، وانصرفنابسقام وما سألنا حكيما

Ḥakīm can mean either 'a wise man' or 'a physician.' The mention of illness suggests the latter, but both senses may be intended.

On the house (dār), line 1
When the cold’s nose ran, you set out; would thatafter our parting that nose had been punished by being cut off!
إذ ذن أنف البرد سرت فليتهعقيب التنائي كان عوقب بالجدع

The unvocalized سرت is read here as “you set out”; “I set out” is also grammatically possible.

On the house (dār), line 2
There, if I fell ill, I would be visitedby women; any who did not come would send word.
هنالك لو أني مرضت لعادنيعوائد من لم يأت منهن يرسل

The object of يرسل ('would send') is unstated: this could mean sending word or sending someone in her place.

On the house (dār), line 1
Do not let the distance to my homelessen my share of your affection.
لا تجلعن بعد داريمخسسا لنصيبي

تجلعن appears to be a transposition error for تجعلن, 'do not make/let.' 'Of your affection' is implicit in نصيبي, literally 'my share.'

On the house (dār), line 2
For many a person far awayis close to the heart,
فرب شخص بعيدإلى الفواد قريب

الفواد is read as الفؤاد, 'the heart,' with the hamza omitted in the source.

On the house (dār), line 1
I have seen that nearness of dwellings is of no useif hearts are not close to one another.
رأيت دنو الدار ليس بنافعإذا لم يكن بين القلوب قريب

The construction «بين القلوب قريب» is unusual; I understand it as expressing closeness between hearts.

On the house (dār), line 6
that is when my messages will be slow to reach you,and there tidings of you will cease.
فهناك حين تريث عنك رسائليوهناك تقطع عنكم الأخبار

تقطع عنكم الأخبار is rendered as news of the addressees ceasing; it could instead mean that news will cease to reach them.

On the house (dār), line 1
My two friends, turn aside today,that you may greet Mayy’s dwelling from atop your riding camels.
خليلي عوجا اليومحتى تسلما على دارمي من صدور الركائب

Read دارمي as دار مي, “Mayy’s dwelling,” with a missing space.

On the house (dār), line 1
O dwelling of Mayya at al-Khalṣāʾ, then al-Jurd,may you be watered, though you stir even the faintest longing in the grief-stricken.
يا دار مية بالخلصاء فالجردسقيا، وإن هجت أدنى الشوق للكمد

I read للكمد as li-l-kamid, referring to a grief-stricken person. If read li-l-kamad, referring to grief itself, أدنى الشوق للكمد could mean 'longing nearest to grief.'

On the house (dār), line 1
Ah, Mayy has departed: there is her dwelling;dark ostriches trot there, and patterned doves.
ألا ظعنت مي فهاتيك دارهابها السحم تردي والحمام الموشم

السحم literally means 'the dark ones'; I take it to mean dark-plumaged ostriches, though the species is not explicit.

On the house (dār), line 5
It is wound enough to the soul, Mayy, that Iand you are among the living, yet do not speak.
كفى حزة في النفس يا مي أننيوإياك في الأحياء لا ننتكلم

في الأحياء is taken as 'among the living'; it could also mean 'among the tribes.'

On the house (dār), line 1
Her dwelling has carried Laylā far from you; you do not visit her.Her destination is far off, and her resolve is firm.
نأتك بليلى دارها لا تزورهاوشطت نواها واستمر مريرها

استمر مريرها evokes a firmly twisted cord and idiomatically suggests firmness of resolve. Here it may instead describe the separation as settled or irrevocable. The pronoun in لا تزورها could refer either to Laylā or to her dwelling.

On the house (dār), line 1
May the rain cloud come early, driven by the south wind,and give you your fill of water, O dwelling of Umāma.
