بكر العارض تحدوه النعامىوسقاك الري يا دار أماما

أماما is taken as a form of the woman's name Umāma (أمامة), apparently shortened and adapted to the rhyme; the transmitted spelling is unusual.

On the house (dār), line 2
Love has wasted him, and his beloved has clothed herself in estrangement;His separation has grown vast, though the place of meeting is near.
طواه الهوى واستشعر الهجر إلفهوشطت نواه والمزار قريب

The beloved’s gender is not specified by إلفه; “herself” is a translation choice.

On the house (dār), line 2
A people who erased my misery and lefttime no power to harm me.
قوم محوا بوسي ولم يتركواعلي للأيام من باس

بوسي and باس appear to represent بؤسي ('my misery') and بأس ('harm' or 'might'), with the hamzas omitted.

On the house (dār), line 2
Hear my words, and do not be angry with me, forin advising you I seek neither money nor worldly gain.
اسمع مقالي، ولا تغضب علي، فماأبغي بنصحك لا مالا ولا عرضا

The unvocalized عرضا is taken as ʿaraḍan, worldly goods or gain; a reading connected with honor or reputation is also possible.

On the house (dār), line 1
You built a house, thinking it a noble deed;may God unleash a flood upon it.
شدت دارا خلتها مكرمةسلط الله عليها الغرقا

The unvocalized خلتها can mean either “you thought it” or “I thought it”; the translation adopts the former.

On the house (dār), line 1
If you fear that an affair may slip beyond your reach, entrust itto another; and move away from an abode of harm.
إذا خفت من أمر فواتا فولهسواك وعن دار الأذى فتحول

فواتًا may refer to missing an opportunity or failing to bring an affair to completion.

On the house (dār), line 7
I let my gaze wander wearily, then turned it backover winter quarters, summer quarters, and places we frequented—
أراسل الطرف وهنا ثم أعطفهفي متشتى ومصطاف ومرتاد

وهنا is taken as 'wearily,' but it could instead be a temporal expression meaning 'late at night.'

On the house (dār), line 1
When my home no longer suited me, I turned away from it;I left it and settled among Juʿf.
لما نبت داري نبوت بهافتركتها ونزلت في جعف

جعف apparently denotes the tribe of Juʿfī in a shortened form, transliterated here as Juʿf.

On the house (bayt), line 1
[And] had I made my mount kneel at Abū Wahb’s abode,she would have departed with her rider not disappointed in his bounty.
[و] لو بأبي وهب أنخت مطيتيغدت من نداه رحلها غير خائب

The Arabic literally says that the mount’s “saddle” (رحلها) would not be disappointed; this is understood as referring to its rider.

On the house (bayt), line 4
Then Quraysh divided the Kaʿba among themselves. The side containing the door fell to Banū ʿAbd Manāf and Zuhra. The stretch between the Black Corner and the Yamānī Corner fell to Banū Makhzūm and those clans of Quraysh that joined them. The back of the Kaʿba fell to Banū Jumaḥ and Sahm, the two sons of ʿAmr ibn Huṣayṣ ibn Kaʿb ibn Luʾayy. The side adjoining the Ḥijr fell to Banū ʿAbd al-Dār ibn Quṣayy, Banū Asad ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā ibn Quṣayy, and Banū ʿAdī ibn Luʾayy; this is the Ḥaṭīm, the site of the idol. Then the people shrank from demolishing it and were afraid to do so. Al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra said, “I shall be the first of you to demolish it.” He took a pickaxe, then stood upon it, saying, “O God, be not alarmed, for we intend only good.” Then he demolished part of it on the side of the two corners. The people waited that night and said, “We shall see: if he is afflicted, we shall demolish nothing and shall restore it as it was. But if nothing befalls him, then God has approved what we have done, and we shall proceed with the demolition.” In the morning al-Walīd went early to his work and continued demolishing, and the people demolished with him, until they reached the foundations of Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him. They uncovered green stones like spearheads, interlocking with one another, [] .
ثم إن قريشا تجزأت الكعبة، فكان شق الباب لبني عبد مناف وزهرة، وكان ما بين الركن الأسود، والركن اليماني لبني مخزوم وقبائل من قريش انضموا إليهم، وكان ظهر الكعبة لبني جمح وسهم، ابني عمرو بن هصيص بن كعب بن لؤي، وكان شق الحجر لبني عبد الدار بن قصي، ولبني أسد بن عبد العزى بن قصي، ولبني عدي بن لؤي، وهو الحطيم موضع الصنم. ثم إن الناس هابوا هدمها، وفرقوا منه، فقال الوليد بن المغيرة: أنا أبدو كم في هدمها، فأخذ المعول، ثم قام عليها وهو يقول: اللهم لم ترع، فإنا لا نريد إلا الخير، ثم هدم من ناحية الركنين، فتربص الناس تلك الليلة، وقالوا: ننظر، إن أصيب لم نهدم شيئا، ورددناها كما كانت، وإن لم يصبه شيء فقد رضي الله بما صنعنا فهدمنا، فأصبح الوليد غاديا على عمله، وهدم وهدم الناس، حتى انتهى الهدم بهم إلى أساس إبراهيم عليه السلام، فأفضوا إلى حجارة خضر كالأسنة أخذ بعضها ببعض، [] .

This entry is prose rather than a poetic line and appears to have been included with the quotation accidentally. Its dangling opening bracket and the closing bracket supplied as h2 have been retained.

On the house (bayt), line 3
its Stone.
حجره

“حجره” (“its Stone”) completes “وضعنا” (“we set in place”) in the preceding line. Its separation as a source line appears to be a formatting error; the supplied division is retained.

On the house (bayt), line 2
The eagle of death flew through its roofed halls,and after its people were gone, it became a place of woe and ruin.
طارت عقاب المنايا في سقائفهفصار من بعدهم للويل والحرب

الحرب is read here as al-ḥarab, meaning despoilment or devastation, hence 'ruin'; the unvocalized text also permits al-ḥarb, 'war.'

On the house (bayt), line 2
Neighbor to dwellers whose abodes are farfrom the living—may rain bless those abodes and their dwellers!
مجاور سكن من ديار بعيدةمن الحي سقيا للديار وللسكن

The construction من ديار بعيدة من الحي is ambiguous. I take it to describe the dead as dwelling far from the living; الحي could also mean 'the tribe,' and من ديار literally means 'from abodes.'

On the house (bayt), line 5
How many a noble clan lies there at al-Ḥajūn,And virtuous elders and young men!
كم بذاك الحجون من [حي صدق]وكهول أعفة وشباب

The source brackets «حي صدق», apparently indicating an editorial restoration. It is rendered as “a noble clan,” though «حي» may instead refer here to a living person or group of people remembered among the dead.

On the house (bayt), line 1
How splendid those dwellings! When you settle there,the poor grow rich, and the offender finds protection.
لله أبيات إذا أوطنتهاغنى الفقير بها، وعز الجاني

غنى appears to represent غني, ‘grew rich.’ عز الجاني could mean that the offender gains honor or enjoys protection; the latter sense is adopted here.

On the house (bayt), line 9
Whoever gains vengeance finds relief, but inmy gaining vengeance lies the loss of him who bereaved me.
يشتفي المدرك بالثأر وفيدركي ثأري ثكل مثكلي

ثكل مثكلي could grammatically mean either losing the person who bereaved her or that person's own bereavement. The translation adopts the former: vengeance for her husband would mean losing her brother Jassās.

On the house (bayt), line 5
Yes, the talebearers spoke truly: you are belovedto me, though your character is not without blemish.
أجل صدق الواشون أنت حبيبةإلي، وإن لم تصف منك الخلائق

وإن لم تصف منك الخلائق may refer specifically to her unkind or troubled dealings with the speaker, rather than to flaws in her character generally.

On the house (bayt), line 2
I shunned you as one shuns the hated, though within youis one person, among all people, dear to me.
هجرتكما هجر البغيض، وفيكمامن الناس إنسان إلى حبيب

The printed إلى حبيب appears to stand for إليّ حبيب, ‘dear to me,’ which is the reading translated here.

On the house (bayt), line 8
I see a woman bearing your name, and she increasesmy longing for you—your namesake, claiming kinship.
وأرى السمية باسمكم فيزيدنيشوقا إليك سميك المتنسب

The text shifts from feminine السمية to masculine سميك المتنسب. I take both expressions to refer to the woman sharing the beloved’s name.

On the house (bayt), line 9
I deal graciously with the tale-bearers concerning you, to keep up appearances,though they harbor grudges against me and are practiced in spite.
وأخالق الواشين منك تجملاوهم على ذوو ضغائن درب

على appears to stand for عليّ, “against me.” The unvocalized درب is taken to mean “practiced” or “experienced”; “in spite” is supplied from the context.

On the house (bayt), line 10
Then you took them as confidants against me, until I grew angry—and such conduct does provoke anger.
ثم اتخذتهم على وليجة حتى غضبت، ومثل ذلك يغضب

على is again read as عليّ, “against me.” The unvocalized verbs are understood as “you took them” and “I grew angry.”

On the house (bayt), line 2
I overlook things you do that distress me,and when summoned to what pleases you, I answer.
وأغضى على أشياء منك تسوءنيوأدعي إلى ما سركم فأجيب

I read «وأغضى» as «وأُغضي» (‘I overlook’) and «وأدعي» as «وأُدعى» (‘I am summoned’); the final ي and ى appear to have been interchanged.

On the house (bayt), line 5
And, weary, with their faces unveiled, they seemedlike eggs heaped around al-Ḥaṭīm.
وكأنهن وقد حسرن لواغبابيض بأكناف الحطيم مركم

«حسرن» can mean that they uncovered themselves, here understood as unveiling their faces, but it can also mean that they became exhausted. «لواغبا» explicitly describes them as weary.

On the house (bayt), line 4
I hope for a second draught of Laylā’s drink, though I have not had a first—how, then, can I have a second?
فآمل أن أعل بشرب ليلى ولم أنهل فكيف لي العلول؟

The phrase بشرب ليلى is ambiguous: it may refer to Laylā’s drink or to drinking with her.

On the house (bayt), line 1
O neighbor of the house whose neighbor is protected,you have departed—who will grant me a noonday resting-place among you?
أيا جارة البيت الممنع جارهرحلت ومن لي عندكم بمقيل

The unvocalized رحلت can mean either “you departed” or “I departed.” I have taken it as addressing the woman, as in the later lines.

On the house (bayt), line 2
Bewildered by parting, you forgot where the necklace belongsand hung it on your cheek and the track of your tears.
نسيت مكان العقد من دهش النوىوعلقته في وجنة ومسيل

نسيت and علقته likewise permit either first-person or second-person readings. The necklace apparently represents tears strung like pearls; مسيل literally means a watercourse or channel, here understood as the tears' track down the cheek.

On the house (bayt), line 3
And may you dwell among folk with no neighborly contact between them,and no reunion unless the dead rise again.
وجاورت قوما لا تجاور بينهمولا وصل إلا أن يكون نشور

جاورت is read as continuing the preceding wish ('may you dwell'), though its unvocalized form could also mean 'you dwelt' or 'I dwelt.'

On the house (bayt), line 3
I said to her—as sudden tears overtook her,
فقلت لهاواستعجلتها بوادر

The source appears to divide a single bayt across entries 3–4: «فقلت لها واستعجلتها بوادر» forms its first hemistich, and «جرت فجرى في جريهن عبير» its second. The supplied divisions are preserved.

On the house (bayt), whole poem

The attribution is inconsistent: the poet field names Jarīr ibn ʿAṭiyyah, while the introduction attributes these verses to al-Farazdaq.

On the house (bayt), line 3
May God send rain upon al-Yamāma, the abode of a people,where ʿAmr longs to be on his way.
سقى الله اليمامة دار قومبها عمرو يحن إلى الرواح

الرواح can denote setting out, especially in the evening, or returning. The verse does not specify whether ʿAmr longs to depart or to return.

On the house (bayt), line 1
You ask—if only you knew ʿAmr’s plight!Who can give you an answer but one who knows?
سألت، ولو علمت بحال عمروومن لك بالجواب سوى الخبير؟

The clause ولو علمت بحال عمرو has no explicit conclusion. It is rendered as a wish, 'if only you knew,' though an unfinished conditional, 'had you known,' is also possible.

On the house (bayt), line 4
I seem to see you, O ʿAmr ibn Kaʿb,as though you had been borne upon a bier.
تخيل لي هيا عمرو بن كعبكأنك قد حملت على السرير

The unvocalized تخيل لي is taken as 'it appears to me'; it could also be read as an imperative, 'appear to me.'

On the house (bayt), whole poem

The attribution is inconsistent: the poet field names Mihyār, while the introduction names al-Buḥturī.

On the house (bayt), line 1
A young man's remaining among his people, alive and safe,in good health, is a state of abasement that demeans him.
مقام الفتى في الحي حيا مسلمامعافى مقام ذلة بالفتى يزري

I read مسلما as musallaman, meaning 'safe' or 'unharmed'; the unvocalized spelling is ambiguous.

On the house (bayt), line 4
Had contentment not brought me a kingdom,the veils and shields protecting me would have been torn away.
لولا القناعة جاءتني بمملكةلهتكت دوني الأستار والجنن

The unvocalized لهتكت is read here as passive, 'would have been torn away.' An active reading, 'I would have torn away,' is also grammatically possible.

On the house (bayt), line 1
A night of dripping rain, with no sleep in it—I lay awake through it until the breaking dawn.
وليلة واكف لا نوم فيهاسهرت بها إلى الصبح الفتيق

واكف can describe falling rain or a dripping roof; the phrase may refer specifically to a night beneath a leaking roof.

On the house (bayt), line 2
When the clouds withdraw from it, its leaks are fed bya pouring cloud whose water never runs dry.
إذا السحب عنه أقلعت فلو كفهسحاب هتون ماؤها ليس ينزف

The spaced wording فلو كفه is read as فَلِوَكْفِهِ, literally ‘for its dripping there is…’; ‘its leaks are fed by’ renders this somewhat unusual construction.

On the house (bayt), line 1
He wants the fat of meat, but meat is not to be had;we have no old she-camel to slaughter, nor a young male camel.
يريد إهال النحض، والنحض معوزوليس لنا ناب يكب ولا بكر

إهال is unusual; I take it as related to إهالة, melted fat or grease. النحض means flesh or lean meat. يكب is understood here as referring to felling a camel for slaughter.

On the house (bayt), line 1
I greet all who dwell in this house,except al-Rabāb: her I do not greet.
حييت ساكن هذا البيت كلهمإلا الرباب، فإني لا أحييها

ساكن ('dweller') is singular, whereas كلهم ('all of them') is plural. It is translated collectively here; the intended reading may be سكان ('dwellers').

On the house (bayt), line 2
She has taken another in my place, knowing wellthat graves conceal those who lie within them.
استبدلت بدلا مني، فقد علمتأن القبور توارى من ثوى فيها

توارى appears to stand for تواري ('conceal'), the reading followed here.

On the house (bayt), line 2
And faces through whose garments shinestheir noble nature—or their lineage.
وأوجها يشف من أثوابهاعنصرها الكريم [أ] ونجارها

The printed '[أ] ونجارها' appears to supply an alif to form أو نجارها ('or their lineage'). Without that addition, it reads 'and their lineage.'

On the house (bayt), line 3
We would give ourselves for you, house: entering you is a delight,and your shade, could it be reached, is cool and pleasant.
بنا أنت من بيت دخولك لذةوظلك لو يسطاع بالبارد السهل

The prefixed bāʾ in بالبارد السهل is grammatically unexpected here; the phrase is taken as describing the shade as 'cool and pleasant.'

On the house (bayt), line 1
Ah, to the dwellings by the sand ridge of ghaḍā trees—to their rooftops or their shade—is there a way?
ألا هل إلى الأبيات بالحبل ذي الغضىذراهن أو أظلالهن سبيل

الحبل ذي الغضى is translated descriptively as 'the sand ridge of ghaḍā trees'; it may instead designate a particular place, Ḥabl Dhī al-Ghaḍā.

On the house (bayt), line 1
Ah, to the dwellings by the sand ridge of ghaḍā trees—to their rooftops or their shade—is there a way?
ألا هل إلى الأبيات بالحبل ذي الغضىذراهن أو أظلالهن سبيل

ذراهن is read as dhurāhunna, 'their upper parts' or 'their rooftops'; the unvocalized text may alternatively refer to their shelter.

On the house (bayt), line 1
I passed by the tents of Kās, and down streamedthe tears of my eyes, while the winds swayed them.
مررت على أبيات كاس فأسبلتمدامع عيني، والرياح تميلها

The pronoun in تميلها, ‘swayed them,’ could refer to the tents or to the tears.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 9
And when the cold winds blew,and night’s blackness drew one household close to another,
وكانوا إذا ما القر هبت رياحهوضم سواد الليل رحلا إلى رحل

رحل can mean a saddle or, by extension, a dwelling or household. I take the image to be households drawing close together at night.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 10
they would make the two jugular veins and the sciatic vein flow with the sword,when no people’s herdsman went out for milk.
يدرون بالسيف الوريدين والنساإذا لم يقم راعي أناس إلى رسل

The bleeding vessels apparently belong to livestock slaughtered to feed others when milk was scarce, but the animals are not explicitly named. النسا is the vessel traditionally called the ‘sciatic vein.’

On weeping for family and brothers, line 2
Had your love been for one alone, you would havedesisted; but your love is divided.
لو كان ما واحدا هواك لقدأقصرت، لكن هواك مشترك

The contrast between واحداً and مشترك is ambiguous: it may mean love directed toward one person versus several, as translated, or one-sided versus mutual love. The particle ما appears to be pleonastic.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 3
Through them we tended the whole community and fed onspring pasture, and relieved the debtor of the burden he bore.
وكنا بهم نرعى الجميع، ونأكل الربيع، ونكفي حامل الغرم ما حمل

نرعى الجميع is ambiguous: it may mean looking after the whole company or pasturing together. The translation adopts the former.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 2
I remembered Banū Sahl, with between me and themthe ravines of al-Ḥimā, its corners and its slopes.
ذكرت بني سهل وبيني وبينهمشراج الحمى أركانه ومناكبه

شراج is understood as ravines or watercourses. الحمى may designate a particular place, provisionally rendered al-Ḥimā, or simply mean protected pastureland.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 5
(“Was allied”etc.): he means that forbearance mingled with their fierceness.
(حالفتإلخ) يريد خالط حدتهم حلم.

This is an explanatory prose gloss on line 4, not a verse. It has been translated in the supplied two-part division.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 3
Al-zaw: destruction and the varying forms of death.
الزو: الهلاك واختلاف المنية

This appears to be an explanatory prose gloss incorporated into the verse list. اختلاف المنية may mean the varying forms or circumstances of death.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
The turns of my fate have begrudged me the blessingof honoring my parents in their graves.
نافستني صروف دهري في الفوز ببر الآباء في الرجم

الرجم is unusual here; I understand it as referring to graves marked or covered with stones.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 4
And injustice on earth denies meeverything I seek—even visiting their mortal remains.
والظلم في الأرض ما نعي كلل ما أبغيه حتى زيارة الرمم

I read ما نعي as مانعي, 'denying me.' The division كل / ل appears to represent the doubled l of كلّ across the hemistich boundary.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 6
One says “a defective substitute” when it is unsound. He means: “This dwelling is a defective substitute for those.”
يقال: خلف أعور، إذا كان فاسدا، يقول: هذا الدار خلف أعور من هاتيك

This source item is an explanatory prose gloss, not a verse. It has been translated in its supplied position. هذا الدار also shows irregular gender agreement.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 2
And how, when they have become bones and graves,whose owls and death-birds cry out at dusk?
وكيف وقد صاروا عظاما وأقبرايصيح صداها بالعشي وهامها؟

“And how” leaves the question incomplete: what is being questioned is not explicit in this excerpt.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 5
After you were gone, enemies turned their gazetoward me, and treacherous times filled me with misgiving.
فبعدك مدت الأعداء طرفاإلى ورابني دهر مريب

The printed إلى appears to stand for إليّ, 'toward me,' which the syntax requires.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 3
The earth dreads their treading upon it;with men like them you make peace or wage war.
تهال الأرض أن يطآ عليهابمثلهما تسالم أو تعادي

تسالم أو تعادي can address an unspecified ‘you’ or have ‘the earth’ as its grammatical subject; the translation takes it as the former.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 4
They have gone, and we follow the way of those who diedamong them: one mourned, another stricken with grief.
ذهبوا، ونحن على طريقة من مضىمنهم، فمفجوع به، ومفجع

The unvocalized مفجع is read here as مُفَجَّع, “stricken with grief,” in contrast to مفجوع به, the person whose loss is mourned.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
Take comfort, for patience better befits a noble man;lamenting the blows of time is of no avail.
تعز فإن الصبر بالحر أجملوليس على ريب الزمان معول

معول can denote lamentation or something to rely upon. The translation takes it here as lamentation that offers no relief.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 2
And of the young man Fajr and Layth, who followed one another in death;after the beloved companion, only acquaintances remained.
وبعد الفتى فجر وليث تتابعافلم يبقى بعد الإلف إلا المعارف

فلم يبقى appears to contain a textual or grammatical error for فلم يبقَ, ‘so none remained.’ الإلف can mean a beloved companion or companionship; the former is adopted here.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
Time has taken my brothers one by one and left meas a hunter leaves a solitary wild bull.
تخرم الدهر إخواني وغادرنيكما يغادر ثور الطارد الفرد

The unvocalized phrase «ثور الطارد الفرد» is syntactically ambiguous. I read «الطارد» as the subject, 'the hunter,' and «ثور … الفرد» as the object, 'a solitary wild bull.'

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
Those who share my grief sleep, as do those who blame me;cares keep me awake, and I keep them awake.
ينام المسعدون ومن يلوموتوقظني وأوقظها الهموم

The unvocalized المسعدون could mean either those who assist or console the mourner, or those blessed with happiness. The translation adopts the former reading.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 2
By day I seem healthy to anyone who sees me,but my night neither sleeps nor lets me sleep.
صحيح بالنهار لمن يرانيوليلى لا ينام ولا ينيم

وليلى is understood as وليلي, 'and my night,' with final ي written as ى.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 5
Whatever my condition, it reminds me of them;so misery and happiness are alike.
يذكرنيهم ما كنت فيهفسيان المساءة والنعيم

ما كنت فيه may refer to the speaker's former circumstances ('what I once enjoyed') rather than, as translated here, whatever condition he finds himself in.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 4
Would that I knew! Was this what we once knew, or were theypeople like others who pass away, and so passed away?
ليت شعري! كذاكم العهد أم كانوا أناسا كمن يزول فزالوا

كذاكم العهد is ambiguous. I understand العهد as the formerly familiar state of things; it could instead mean a pledge or bond of loyalty.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 3
This world will not endure, nor will there remain in ita single watchful eye among the living.
فما الدنيا بقائمة وفيهامن الأحياء من عين رموق

The scope of the negation in «فما الدنيا بقائمة وفيها…» is ambiguous. The translation takes it to deny permanence both to the world and to any living inhabitant.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
I have known and tested life's affairs, and I do not seein the one who comes after the equal of the departed whom he follows.
عرفت، وجربت الأمور فما أرىكماض تلاه الغابر المتأخر

The syntax is ambiguous without case endings. I take الغابر المتأخر ('the one who remains behind') as the delayed object of أرى, compared unfavorably with his departed predecessor; تلاه then means 'whom he follows.'

On weeping for family and brothers, line 3
Now the man I used to remember in prosperity—indeed, whom I never forget—forgets me in adversity.
وصار من كنت في السراء أذكرهبل لست أنساه في الضراء ينساني

The phrase في الضراء ('in adversity') could alternatively qualify 'I never forget him,' giving: '—indeed, whom I never forget in adversity—now forgets me.'

On weeping for family and brothers, line 4
I excuse people who, were I to summon any of thembefore his own conscience, would lower his eyes, too ashamed to offer an excuse.
واعذر قوما لو أحاكم بعضهمإلى نفسه أغضى حياء من العذر

The phrase «حياء من العذر» is ambiguous: it may mean being too ashamed to offer an excuse, as translated, or feeling ashamed at the excuse or pardon offered on his behalf.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
Between al-Ḥarīsh and Tall Maḥrā lie buriedhorsemen of Nimārah, never wavering.
ثوى بين الحريش وتل محرىفوارس من نمارة غير ميل

Mīl (ميل), translated as 'wavering,' can describe riders unsteady in the saddle or, by extension, cowardly men.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 2
Would that I knew, now that Barmak’s house has passed awayand the joyous, happy man has become grief-stricken:
يا ليت شعري إذا ما برمك درجتوأصبح الفرح المسرور ذا كمد

The feminine verb درجت appears to treat برمك as a collective referring to Barmak’s family, the Barmakids; hence “Barmak’s house.”

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
After the Banū Bakr, shall I hope for anything yet to comefrom time, or grieve over the loss of what has passed?
أبعد بني بكر أؤمل مقبلامن الدهر أو آسى على فقد مدبر؟

The excerpt does not establish which group called Banū Bakr is intended.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 3
O eye, weep for the defenders of glory, and weepfor those who shelter the offender and protect the womenfolk.
عين فابكي الحماة للمجد، وابكيمن يجير الجاني ويحمي الحريما

Ḥarīm, translated as 'womenfolk,' can also mean more broadly those things or persons held inviolable and entitled to protection.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
May treacherous Time find no pleasure in its food,nor swallow with ease—how much it has devoured!
لا يهنأ الدهر الخئون، ولا أساغ، فكم أكل

The spelling الخئ / ون appears to represent الخؤون, “treacherous,” with the word divided between hemistichs. “In its food” is implicit in the wish expressed by لا يهنأ and the following imagery of swallowing and devouring.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 2
Time struck down its equal:a champion matched against a champion.
فتك الزمان بمثلهبطل أتيح له بطل

I take بمثله to mean that Time slew someone equal to itself, making Time and the deceased the two champions. The compressed wording leaves this comparison somewhat ambiguous.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 5
I shall weep for my dear companions, who drew forthmy tears drop by drop, until grief swiftly ravaged my mind.
سأبكي أخلائي الذي تبرضوادموعي، حتى أسرع الحزن في عقلي

الذي does not agree with the plural أخلائي and تبرضوا; الذين appears to be intended.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
I say to her,when she forbids me to weep:
أقول لهالما نهتني عن البكا

This is much shorter than a complete bayt in the stated meter and appears to be a fragment or an irregularly divided line.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 6
Would that I could have enjoyed his company for a lifetime,at the price of all my wealth, newly acquired and inherited,
بودي لو أني تمليت عمرهبمالي من مال طريف وتالد

The phrase تمليت عمره is unusual: literally it suggests enjoying his lifetime. I take it to mean enjoying his continued companionship, with the following phrases imagining his life redeemed by wealth and a hand.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 3
men in their prime and beardless youths among Mālik’s kinsmen,and trusty, generous gamesters—worthy companions, had you long enjoyed their company.
كهول ومرد من بني عم مالكوأيسار صدق لو تمليتهم رضى

The construction لو تمليتهم رضى is compressed. تمليتهم may address “you” or refer to “I”; رضى is understood as describing men worthy of approval.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 6
with its soul-destroying arrows:whenever they strike a life, they snatch it away.
بأسهمها المتلفات النفومتى ما تصب مهجة تخلس

النفو appears to be missing the final س of النفوس, ‘souls.’ Unlike the divided word in line 3, the missing letter does not appear at the beginning of the second hemistich.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 7
They struck them down in the reaches of desolation,left lying upon the earth, unburied.
فصرعنهم بنواحي البلاملقى بأرض ولم يرمس

البلا may represent البلاء, ‘affliction,’ or البلى, ‘decay’; ‘desolation’ is provisional. The second hemistich has singular ملقى and يرمس after plural ‘them,’ which may indicate textual damage.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 2
Here is Abū al-Qāsim, lying in a barren waste;the winds scatter their drifting dust over him.
هذا أبو القاسم الثاوي ببلقعةتسفي الرياح عليه من سوافيها

I could not establish the identity of Abū al-Qāsim.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
Tell me: scarcely do the wounds of grief healfor one friend before I am bereaved of another?
أجدك ما تعفوا كلوم مصيبةعلى صاحب إلا فجعت بصاحب؟

تعفوا appears to stand for تعفو ('heal' or 'fade'), with an extra final alif.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 6
Now that the earth has shut him away,despite his nearness, I am as though I had never been his companion.
فأصبحت لما حالت الأرض دونهعلى قربه مني كمن لم أصاحب

The construction كمن لم أصاحب is awkward: literally, 'like someone I never accompanied.' It is understood here as expressing that burial has separated the friends as though their companionship had never existed.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 2
Whenever I turn inward and speak to myselfof those companions of mine whom the pits have enclosed,
إذا رجعت إلى نفسي أحدثهاعمن تضمن من أصحابي القلب

I read القلب as القُلُب, the plural of قليب ('well' or 'pit'), as supported by the meter. These appear to be burial pits, though literal wells may be intended.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 2
Now that the Banū Umayya have departed from it,and the noble lords of the Banū ʿAbd Shams.
حين غابت بنو أمية عنهاوالبهاليل من بني عبد شمس

The feminine pronoun in ʿanhā ('from it') has no explicit feminine antecedent in the excerpt; it presumably refers to the place mentioned as al-Khayf.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 3
Orators upon the pulpits,knights upon them, eloquent speakers, never tongue-tied.
خطباء على المنابر فرسان، عليها، وقالة غير خرس

ʿalayhā ('upon them') appears to refer to the pulpits, making 'knights upon them' a metaphor for mastery in public speaking.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 3
I remain beside your graves and will not leave,through the long nights, until your echo answers.
أقيم على قبريكما لست بارحاطوال الليالي أو يجيب صداكما

صداكما is rendered as “your echo,” but ṣadā can also denote the owl associated in pre-Islamic belief with the dead person's spirit. That sense may be intended here.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 3
I remain beside your graves and will not leavethrough the long nights, until your echoes answer.
مقيما على قبريكما، لست بارحاطوال الليالي أو يجيب صداكما

صداكما is rendered 'your echoes.' Ṣadā can also denote an owl associated in pre-Islamic belief with the dead; that sense may be intended here.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
Do not deny a dead man's spirit its drink;give him wine to drink, though he is buried.
لا تصرد هامة عن شربهاواسقه الراح وإن كان قبر

Hāmah can mean a skull or the bird believed to embody a dead person's spirit; I have taken it in the latter sense. Tuṣarrid may mean to stint someone's drink rather than withhold it entirely.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 4
Whoever death has hidden from sight,it will return in his wake.
ومن تكن المنية غيبتهفسوف على تفيئته تعود

The uncommon expression على تفيئته is understood as 'in his wake' or 'following after him': apparently death will return for those the deceased has left behind.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 4
Then Muḥammad ibn Ṣāliḥ died—may God have mercy on him.
فتوفى محمد بن صالحرحمه الله

This appears to be the compiler’s prose reporting the poet’s death, not a verse of the poem. It has been translated in the supplied divisions.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 9
May the grave in which noble Ibn Ṣāliḥ nowdwells be watered by a low-hanging cloud pouring rain.
سقى جدثا أمسى الكريم ابن صالحيحل به دان من المزن ساكب

The identity of Ibn Ṣāliḥ cannot be established from the supplied excerpt.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 8
By God, I shall never meet their likeuntil I am held captive by the grave:
تالله ألقى الدهر مثلهمحتى أكون رهينة القبر

The supplied text has no explicit negative before ألقى. I understand the oath as implying an omitted لا: “I shall never meet their like.”

On weeping for family and brothers, line 14
How many a brother have you lost—one who stood through his night in prayer until dawn,
كم من أخ لك قد فجعت بهقوام ليلته إلى الفجر

The unvocalized فجعت here and رزئتهم in line 18 permit either first- or second-person readings. I take this line as an address and line 18 as first-person, following its explicit “my hand.”

On weeping for family and brothers, line 4
If you two join in my grief, we shall mourn bygone days with tears;yet our weeping and sobbing are little enough to offer him.
فإن تسعدا نندب عهدا بعبرةوقل له منا البكا والتنحب

عهدا can mean a former time or a bond; it is rendered here as 'bygone days.' The pronoun in له ('for him') appears to refer to the deceased rather than to عهد.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 5
How many a worthy clan lies in that al-Ḥajūn,and upright men of mature years, and youths!
كم بذاك الحجون من حي صدقوكهول أعفة، وشباب

حي صدق is taken as 'a worthy clan'; حي can denote a tribal community, though the reference here may be more broadly to worthy people buried at al-Ḥajūn.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 4
Whenever their names are mentioned, or they are called by them,the stout bones of my breast almost split apart.
إذا ذكرت أسماؤهم، أودعوا بهاتكاد حيازيمي تفرى صلابها

I read أودعوا بها as أو دُعوا بها, “or they are called by them,” with a missing space, rather than أُودعوا بها, “they were deposited in it.”

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
They called to one another and said, “The horsemen have felled a rider!”I said, “Is that fallen man ʿAbd Allah?”
تنادوا، فقالا: أردت الخيل فارسافقلت: أعبد الله ذلكم الردى؟

الردى is understood here as الردي (Al-radī), “the slain man,” with an undotted final yāʾ, rather than al-radā, “death.”

On weeping for family and brothers, line 4
Time’s two youths came upon them morning and evening:day and night, overtaking each successive generation.
غدا فتيا دهر، وراحا عليهمنهار وليل يلحقان التواليا

يلحقان التواليا may mean ‘overtaking those who follow’ or, with a causative reading, ‘making those who follow join their predecessors.’ The translation takes التوالي to refer to successive generations.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 16
I recite to people, but do not search for them;only one who has lost something searches for it.
أنشد الناس، ولا أنشدهمإنما ينشد من كان أضل

The unvocalized أنشد permits different readings. The translation takes the first as أُنْشِدُ, 'I recite,' and the second as أَنْشُدُ, 'I seek.' The first could instead mean 'I seek' or 'I inquire of'; 'them' is taken to refer to the dead people.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 3
They carried off my seven brothers,then turned upon my nearest kin,
أتين على إخوتي سبعةوعدن على ربعي الأقرب

ربعي may refer to the poet’s dwelling or household; here I take ربعي الأقرب to mean his nearest kin.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
Night and day struck the women of Āl Ḥarbwith a stroke of fate that left them dazed with grief.
رمى المحدثان نسوة آل حرببمقدار سمدن له سمودا

سمدن له سمودا is understood here as being dazed or bewildered with grief; the verb has several other senses. المحدثان, literally 'the two bringers of change,' denotes night and day.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 4
you would have wept like a bereaved woman wailingwhose only child fate had struck down.
بكيت بكاء معولة فقيدأصاب الدهر واحدها الفقيدا

واحدها, literally 'her only one,' is taken here to mean her only child; the relationship is not explicitly stated.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 1
May God curse an age whose evil is nearer than its good,and the fortune that took Ṣayfī away after Maʿbad.
لحى الله دهرا شره دون خيرهوجدا بصيفي نأى بعد معبد

I read وجدا as wa-jaddan, 'and a fortune,' continuing the curse. The unvocalized text could also represent wajdan, 'grief,' though its syntax would be less clear.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 4
As though Ṣayfī, that faithful brother, and I had never saidto one kindling a fire at the end of the night…
كأني وصيفيا أخا الصدق لم نقللموقد نار آخر الليل

The second hemistich appears incomplete: it lacks the expected rhyme, and the words addressed to the person kindling the fire are missing. The ellipsis marks this apparent omission.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 5
Or that I would live on, my backleft maimed after my brothers were gone.
أو أنني أبقى وظهري بعد إخواني أجب

أجب means shorn of, or lacking, a hump. Applied here to the speaker's back, it appears to suggest the loss of his brothers as a source of support; 'maimed' renders that apparent sense.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 3
If I see them, I shall never turn away from them,save for travel, until I disappear into the grave.
فإن أرهم لا أصدف الدهر عنهمسوى سفر حتى أغيب في القبر

The attachment of “until I disappear into the grave” is ambiguous: it may qualify his lifelong refusal to leave them, apart from travel, or describe the exceptional journey as death itself.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 3
I shoot, but cannot strike dead; and if shots are aimedmy way, I am struck with my throat exposed.
أمري، فلا أصمي، وإن رميتجهتي رميت معرض النحر

أمري appears to be a transposition error for أرمي, ‘I shoot,’ adopted here. Both occurrences of رميت are read as passive: رُمِيَتْ جهتي, ‘shots are aimed my way,’ and رُمِيتُ, ‘I am struck.’

On weeping for family and brothers, line 4
I shrink from meeting the enemy; how could Imeet the enemy when you no longer stand behind me?
وأصد عن لقيا العدو، وهلألقى العدو، ولست من ظهري؟

The unusual phrase ولست من ظهري is read as addressing the deceased, لستَ, with ظهري understood figuratively as support or protection.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 6
And from it, when it descends,there is no deliverance, no escape.
وما عنه إذا ما حلل، لا منجى، ولا مهرب

The isolated ل at the beginning of the second hemistich appears to complete حلّ ('descends') in the first; the divided word is translated wholly in the first hemistich.

On weeping for family and brothers, line 8
If I weep, it is because they were my strength,my pillar and my support.
فإن أبك، فهم عزىوهم ركني، وهم منكب

منكب literally means 'shoulder.' In parallel with 'my strength' and 'my pillar,' it is understood as 'my shoulder/support,' although the possessive ending is not written.
